0.content: The blueprint is the automation each room runs. This page covers every input and how a room behaves. 1.title: Room
1.content: | Input | Default | Description | . | Schedule | required | The FLARE schedule the room follows. | . | Lights & Occupancy | required | The room’s lights, and the occupancy and motion sensors that turn them on and off. An illuminance sensor picked here, or in its area, drives Lux Threshold. | . Lights & Occupancy takes an area, a floor, a device, a label, or individual entities. An area includes lights and sensors added to it later. FLARE picks the room’s lights the same way Home Assistant does when you call light.turn_on on that target: . | A light you pick by name is always included. | A hidden light is left out if it was picked through an area, floor, device or label. | A configuration or diagnostic light, such as the indicator light on a wall switch, is left out if it was picked through an area, floor or device, or a label on its device or area. If the label is on the light itself, it’s included. | . The room’s flare controls the same lights. Sensors are binary_sensor entities with device_class: occupancy or device_class: motion; other binary sensors in the target are ignored. A room can mix both kinds. To pick an area for its lights but leave some of its sensors out, add them with Exclude target (Home Assistant 2026.11 and later). On earlier versions, turn off Sensors From Areas and pick the sensors you want by name. A room with no sensor follows the schedule but never turns its lights on or off. A room can have two automations, for example one for a lamp and one for the ceiling light. Each releases the lights it drives once they’re all off; a light in both is released when either room goes dark.

2.title: Sensors and triggers
2.content: | Input | Default | Description | . | Wait time | 120s | How long every sensor must be clear before the room is empty. Only used when the room has sensors. | . | Lux Threshold | 0 (off) | Above 0, the room leaves its lights off while every illuminance sensor in it reads above this many lux. | . | Additional Triggers | none | Entities that make the room update as soon as they change. | . Lux Threshold . Illuminance sensors are the sensor entities with device_class: illuminance in Lights & Occupancy — picked by name, or included through its area, floor, device or label — that aren’t excluded. With Sensors From Areas off, only the ones picked by name count. Above 0, the room counts as bright enough while every one of those sensors reads above that many lux. A bright room isn’t switched on by: . | a sensor detecting someone, | a scene, unless every light it covers is already on, | idle brightness. | . If someone is still in the room when it stops being bright enough, because one of those sensors drops to the threshold or below, the lights come on then. Someone counts as in the room if one of its occupancy or motion sensors is detecting them, or was within the Wait time. Lights already on carry on as before: following the curve, or left to the phase’s scene. Nothing is switched off for being bright. Turning the room on by hand — the automation’s Run, the flare, or a voice assistant — ignores the threshold. A sensor that is unavailable, unknown or not numeric can’t say how bright the room is, so it doesn’t count either way, and a room with no illuminance sensor never blocks. The check is off while Lux Threshold is 0, which is the default. Additional triggers . Add any entity a template depends on, such as the TV in a Brightness Template that dims the room while it’s playing. An additional trigger only adjusts lights that are already on. To turn a room on from something else, see lighting a room from a remote.

3.title: Brightness
3.content: | Input | Default | Description | . | Lights Off During Morning / Day / Evening / Night | none | Lights to turn off during that phase. | . | Brightness Template | none | A template returning a mapping of entity ID to brightness. Overrides the lists above for the lights it includes. | . Brightness Template values: . | Value | Effect | . | 1–255 | Sets the light to this brightness, on the same scale as the phase brightnesses. | . | 0 | Turns the light off. | . | null | FLARE leaves the light alone, including when the room empties. | . 4.title: Idle brightness
4.content: | Input | Default | Description | . | Morning / Day / Evening / Night Idle Brightness | 0 | The brightness, 0–255, the room’s lights dim to when it empties during that phase. 0 turns them off. | . | Idle Brightness Template | none | Like Brightness Template, for when the room is empty. Overrides the settings above for the lights it includes. | . For a nightlight whenever it’s dark outside, leave the four settings at 0 and set the template to: . {{ 10 if is_state('sun.sun', 'below_horizon') else {} }} . An idle brightness is the only way the room’s lights come on while it’s empty. See Templates for one lamp as the nightlight, and other variations.

5.title: Scenes
5.content: | Input | Default | Description | . | Morning / Day / Evening / Night Scene | none | A scene the room uses instead of the schedule during that phase. | . | Scene Template | none | A template returning a scene’s entity ID, or '' for none. 6.content: | Input | Default | Description | . | Motion On Transition | 1s | Transition when someone comes in, or when you run the automation by hand. | . | Motion Off Transition | 15s | Transition when the room empties. | . | Background Transition | 5s | Transition for every other update. | .

7.title: Settings
7.content: | Input | Default | Description | . | Override Protection | on | Leaves a light alone once something else changes it, until all of the room’s lights are off. | . | Prefer RGB During | Evening, Night | Phases in which lights that support RGB are sent an RGB colour instead of a colour temperature. | . | Stored Traces | 20 | How many of the automation’s recent runs keep a trace. | . | Sensors From Areas | on | Off, sensors aren’t inferred from the areas, floors, devices or labels in Lights & Occupancy; only explicitly selected sensors are used. Deprecated: use Exclude target instead of turning this off. | . Override protection . Turn it off for a room whose bulbs misreport. Prefer RGB during . Many bulbs give richer warm colours in RGB, but their cool whites can look blue, so the default leaves Morning and Day on colour temperature. Stored traces . A room updates every minute, so the default keeps about the last 20 minutes of runs in the automation’s Traces. Raise it while you’re tracking down something that happened earlier; each trace takes memory, so set it back once you’re done. Sensors from areas . Turn Sensors From Areas off and only the sensors you pick by name in Lights & Occupancy count, so you can pick an area for its lights and choose the sensors yourself, such as the hallway’s for a landing. Pick none for a room that only follows the schedule. Sensors From Areas is deprecated, and FLARE 3.0 removes it. From Home Assistant 2026.11, use Exclude target in Lights & Occupancy instead of turning it off, to leave out the sensors you don’t want (see Home Assistant’s excluding targets). An excluded sensor doesn’t count, whether it came from an area, a device, a floor or a label.

8.title: How a room behaves
8.content: When the room updates . A room updates straight away when the phase changes, a sensor detects someone or an Additional Trigger changes, and a few seconds after its lights come back online. Between those, it updates on the tick of the first area in Lights & Occupancy, which is every minute by default. A room whose Lights & Occupancy names no area updates every minute, on the minute. When lights turn on and off . Lights turn on when a sensor detects someone, and turn off once every sensor in the room has been clear for the Wait time. While every light in Lights & Occupancy is off, the only things that turn any of them on are a sensor detecting someone, running the automation by hand, the room getting dark while someone is in it (with a Lux Threshold), and idle brightness. Once at least one light is on, any update can turn on the others. This means a phase change doesn’t light up an empty room, and a bulb that comes back online stays off if the rest of the room is off. If a light is still on after the room has been empty for the Wait time, the turn-off is sent again. Running the automation by hand sets every light in the room, including ones someone else has changed. Why didn’t my light change? . | Someone else changed it. A light changed from a wall switch, an app, a voice assistant or another automation, including being turned off, is left alone until every light in the room is off. See override protection. | The room is empty and the light was off. See when lights turn on and off. | It’s already close enough. Changes smaller than 5% of the brightness or 5 mireds of colour temperature aren’t sent. You can change both tolerances under FLARE → Settings → Configure. | It’s unavailable. FLARE sets it once it comes back online. | A scene has it, or Brightness Template returns null for it. | It’s at its idle brightness. See idle brightness. | It isn’t one of the room’s lights. A hidden light, or a configuration or diagnostic light, isn’t included through an area, floor, device or label. Pick it directly in Lights & Occupancy to include it. See Room. | .

9.title: Turning override protection off
9.content: Override protection works by reading back what each light reports, and checking it against what FLARE last sent. Bulbs don’t always report what they’re actually showing. Some send an old value for a moment after they reconnect, some report a colour in a different form from the one they were sent, and some settle on a colour outside the range they say they support. When a bulb reports something FLARE didn’t send, it reads as overridden even though nobody touched it, and FLARE leaves it alone until every light in the room is off. If a room’s lights keep getting stuck like this, you can turn off Override Protection in the room’s automation. FLARE then sets the room’s lights on every update without checking what they report, which also means: . | A light someone else changes, from a wall switch, an app or another automation, goes back to the curve at the next update. | A light switched off by hand comes back on at the next update while the room is occupied. | If you set the room’s flare to a brightness or colour, for example by asking a voice assistant for 100%, the room goes back to the curve at the next update. Turning the flare on and off works as usual. | . A room with override protection off isn’t counted in the Overrides view. If you turn override protection off because of your bulbs, please open an issue with their make and model, so FLARE can learn to read them properly.

10.title: Updating the blueprint
10.content: The blueprint comes with FLARE, so after each FLARE update a repair appears under Settings → System → Repairs offering the new copy. Press Fix to install it; your automations keep their settings. If you’ve edited your own copy, ignore the repair, because installing replaces the file. FLARE installs the blueprint in Home Assistant’s language (Settings → System → General) when it has a translation for it, so far German, and in English otherwise. If you change Home Assistant’s language, the same repair offers the blueprint in the new one. Its Details links lead to this page, in English. The test trace reports show runs of the blueprint from its tests, with each step matched to the line of the blueprint it comes from.

11.title: Claims and override protection
11.content: Part of Architecture, for contributors and the curious. Nothing here is needed to use FLARE. Override protection is FLARE leaving a light alone once someone else has changed it. It hangs on one question, asked fresh on every write: is this light still showing what FLARE last did to it? The answer comes from comparing the light’s live state with a record of FLARE’s own writes, its claims. There’s no “overridden” flag set once by a trigger. A trigger firing once blocks only the run it fires in (lesson 2 in CLAUDE.md). Re-asking against live state every time is what makes everything else fall out: room-empty, light-off and reconnect releases all just happen.

12.title: The pieces
12.content: | Module | Holds | Pure? | . | tracking/override_protection.py | classify(), the decision table, and classify_state(), its adapter for a live HA state | yes | . | tracking/matching.py | shows(): does a light’s report match a target? | yes | . | tracking/claims.py | ClaimRegistry: claims, rooms, the Store, the state listener | no | . | sensor.py | ClaimEvents (statuses, events), the counts, each light’s status sensor | no | .

13.title: The data
13.content: classDiagram class ClaimRegistry { claims: dict~entity_id, WriteRecord~ rooms: dict~room_key, Room~ status(entity_id) async_record(room, lights, context, targets) adopt(room, lights) async_override(room, lights) async_clear(lights) } class WriteRecord { observed: ContextClaim | None latest: ContextClaim | None mismatch_since: iso | absent } class ContextClaim { context_id secondary_context_id recorded_at target: dict | None } class Room { lights: list~entity_id~ } ClaimRegistry "1" --> "*" WriteRecord ClaimRegistry "1" --> "*" Room WriteRecord --> ContextClaim : observed WriteRecord --> ContextClaim : latest . One claim per light, whichever caller wrote it, so two automations driving the same light never mistake each other’s writes for overrides. Two claims in each record: . | latest is FLARE’s most recent write, not yet seen landing. | observed is a state FLARE can safely write over: a write it has seen land, or for a light’s first-ever write, the context it had just before. | . On each new write, if the light’s live context matches latest, that write landed and is promoted to observed. If it still matches observed, the write never landed and observed stays as it was. Either way the light is still FLARE’s, so a dropped write can’t lock FLARE out. A target is what a write asked for: {brightness, color_temp_kelvin}, {brightness, rgb_color}, or {state: off} for a turn-off. A light reported under a stranger’s context is still FLARE’s if it shows the target. That covers a bulb reporting after HA has forgotten the write’s context, which happens 5 seconds after the call. A room is the caller naming itself: room_id, which for the blueprint is the automation, keyed by its entity-registry id so a rename keeps it. Its lights are the latest room_entities it named, plus whatever it wrote, plus any light it still holds a claim on, so every claim it made can be released with it. A call with no room_id writes but records nothing, and doesn’t read claims either. That’s the blueprint’s Override Protection switch.

14.title: Deciding: classify()
14.content: flowchart TB S(["light state + record"]) --> R{"reachable?"} R -->|"no"| UN["unavailable"] R -->|"yes"| NC{"any claim?"} NC -->|"no"| ONQ{"on?"} ONQ -->|"yes"| UT1["untracked"] ONQ -->|"no"| OFF["off"] NC -->|"yes"| CTX{"live context =<br/>latest or observed?"} CTX -->|"yes"| CON1["controlled"] CTX -->|"no"| ISON{"on?"} ISON -->|"no"| ASKOFF{"a claim asked for off?"} ASKOFF -->|"yes"| CON2["controlled"] ASKOFF -->|"no, no observed"| UT2["untracked"] ASKOFF -->|"no"| OV1["disagrees"] ISON -->|"yes"| OBS{"observed exists?"} OBS -->|"no"| UT3["untracked"] OBS -->|"yes"| VAL{"shows latest's or<br/>observed's target?"} VAL -->|"yes"| CON3["controlled"] VAL -->|"no"| OV2["disagrees"] OV1 --> GR{"mismatch_since older<br/>than 30 s?"} OV2 --> GR GR -->|"yes"| OVR["overridden"] GR -->|"no"| MM["mismatched"] . overridden and mismatched both block: grouping leaves the light out unless the call has force. The difference is only in what’s reported. A light becomes overridden once its mismatch has lasted 30 seconds (MISMATCH_GRACE). Until then it’s mismatched: blocked, so a real change is never written over, but not counted or announced. Most short mismatches are FLARE’s own write still landing, or a bulb reporting a stale value as it reconnects. Being switched off is an override. classify() doesn’t short-circuit on off. FLARE’s own turn-offs record {state: off} as their target, which is how a room switched off at bedtime can come on again but a lamp switched off by hand stays off. Everything that judges a light goes through classify_state(). Grouping calls it through EntityLookup.externally_set(), and the sensors and claims_check through ClaimRegistry.status(). They drifted apart twice when each did its own, and test_one_classifier_adapter.py fails if anything else calls classify(). What a light “shows” (matching.py) . | Reading | Rule | . | brightness | brightness, within the Settings entry’s tolerance (5% by default), never less than 2 | . | Kelvin | color_temp_kelvin; else a white’s xy_color read as Kelvin if it’s within 0.02 Duv of the Planckian locus; never RGB | . | same mired | two Kelvins that floor to the same mired are the same to a Zigbee bulb | . | near mired | within the Settings entry’s tolerance (5 mireds by default), about the smallest change anyone notices | . | out-of-range target | match the target as asked, or clamped to the bulb’s advertised range | . | RGB | rgb_color, only against an RGB target: the channels’ differences summed, within twice the colour tolerance (10 at the default), never less than 4 | . Never Kelvin by way of RGB: HA’s Kelvin→RGB and xy→RGB conversions differ by about 13 in red at 6500K, so a bulb showing exactly what was asked would read as something else.

15.title: A light’s life
15.content: stateDiagram-v2 direction LR [*] --> off: no claim off --> untracked: switched on, no claim untracked --> controlled: FLARE writes (claim recorded)<br/>or adopts it off --> controlled: FLARE switches it on controlled --> controlled: FLARE writes again,<br/>light reports back controlled --> mismatched: shows something else mismatched --> controlled: matches again mismatched --> overridden: after 30 s overridden --> controlled: forced write<br/>(manual run, flare "on") overridden --> untracked: claims_clear / Clear controlled --> [*]: room goes dark → released overridden --> [*]: room goes dark → released controlled --> unavailable: drops out → claim dropped unavailable --> untracked: back online .

16.title: The listener
16.content: ClaimRegistry.async_start_listening follows exactly the claimed lights, through async_track_state_change_event, and re-subscribes whenever the set of claimed lights changes. It follows their registry entries too, with async_track_entity_registry_updated_event. For each change to one: . | Change | Effect | . | any change | note_mismatch: set mismatch_since when it first disagrees, clear it when it matches again | . | on/off → unavailable/unknown (dropped) | its claim is deleted, so its reconnect isn’t read as an override; its rooms are checked for release | . | on/off → off (went off) | each room containing it is released if none of its claimed lights is on | . | none/unavailable/unknown → on/off (arrived) | each room is released if every claimed light has now reported and none is on | . | renamed in the registry | its claim and its place in its rooms move to the new entity ID | . | deleted from the registry | its claim and its place in its rooms go | . The rules the listener keeps: . | Nothing reported while HA is stopping counts. MQTT marks lights unavailable as it disconnects, which would drop every claim just before the Store’s final save. | went_off needs a real starting state. Lights reconnect one at a time after a restart, and the first back being off while its siblings are still unknown mustn’t release the room. | Unavailable counts as dark for release, so one dead bulb can’t hold a room open forever. Only claimed lights count, so a TV backlight the room doesn’t drive can’t either. | .

17.title: Releasing a room
17.content: Once none of a room’s claimed lights is on, the room lets go of all of them (_release_if_dark). That’s deliberate: a light then switched on by hand, or back from unavailable, has no claim, reads untracked, and FLARE takes it to the curve. Keeping your own setting in a dark room is what a flare is for. A light in two rooms is released when either goes dark. Lights that went off while HA wasn’t watching never send an on → off, so claims restored from storage get a settled check (release_settled_dark_rooms): once every claimed light in the room has reported on or off, and none is on.

18.title: Persistence
18.content: flowchart LR ch["any claim change"] --> ds["Store.async_delay_save(5 s)"] ds --> file[".storage/flare.claims<br/>{claims, rooms, overrides}"] stop["EVENT_HOMEASSISTANT_FINAL_WRITE"] --> file file --> load["next start:<br/>async_load before platforms"] load --> seed["ClaimEvents.start():<br/>seed statuses, note mismatches"] seed --> rel["release rooms restored dark"] . | A restart gives every light a fresh context, so a restored claim can only match by value. A light still showing FLARE’s target stays controlled; one changed before the restart keeps its stored mismatch_since, so it’s overridden at once. | A light deleted while HA was down never sends a registry event. Its restored claim counts as dark, and goes when its room next does. | A crash loses the last 5 seconds of claims and fails open: an unclaimed light is free to drive. | overrides is the override log (log_override): the last 50 overrides, each with both claims, the live values, the light’s raw colour attributes (matching.reported()), its device’s manufacturer and model, the integration providing it and the tolerances in force. Logged when ClaimEvents fires flare_light_overridden, which carries part of the same entry. Only the Settings entry’s diagnostics read it. | .

19.title: Showing it
19.content: Where the claims are kept (the registry and its Store) is separate from how they’re shown, and nothing that shows them holds state of its own. | Each room light has a status sensor, sensor.<light>_flare_status, on the light’s own device: what classify_state says, with claimed, asked (FLARE’s last target, unrecorded) and rooms. It updates on its light’s state changes and on SIGNAL_CLAIMS_UPDATED. | The counts, sensor.flare_controlled_lights and sensor.flare_overridden_lights, on FLARE’s own device. untracked counts as controlled, since either way the light isn’t excluded. | The claim events, fired by ClaimEvents: | . | Event | When | Filed under | . | flare_lights_controlled | a room takes lights it wasn’t driving, gathered for 3 s, lit lights only | the Controlled count | . | flare_light_overridden | a light becomes overridden, with both claims and its live values | the Overridden count | . | flare_lights_released | a room goes dark, or Clear | button.flare_clear | . Each event carries one of FLARE’s entities as entity_id and FLARE’s device_id. That’s how they reach FLARE’s Activity, and how the dashboard tells the three kinds apart. A light going back to controlled after an override is churn, not news, and is silent. The first refresh after start seeds the statuses without firing, so a restart doesn’t announce anything.

20.title: Building without the blueprint
20.content: The blueprint is one way to use FLARE’s services. Anything that can call a Home Assistant action — an automation, a script, Node-RED, AppDaemon — can use them directly. On this page . | The smallest automation | Sending the commands yourself | .

21.title: The smallest automation
21.content: You need a schedule for the values. If you want FLARE to leave hand-set lights alone, pass the automation itself as the room. This keeps the kitchen on the curve: . alias: Kitchen lighting triggers: - trigger: event event_type: flare_tick event_data: area_id: kitchen conditions: - condition: template value_template: "{{ area_entities('kitchen') | select('match', '^light\\.') | select('is_state', 'on') | list | count > 0 }}" actions: - action: flare.apply_lighting data: entities: "{{ area_entities('kitchen') | select('match', '^light\\.') | select('is_state', 'on') | list }}" brightness: "{{ state_attr('sensor.home_flare', 'brightness') }}" color_temp_kelvin: "{{ state_attr('sensor.home_flare', 'color_temp') }}" transition: 5 room_id: "{{ this.entity_id }}" room_entities: "{{ area_entities('kitchen') | select('match', '^light\\.') | list }}" . It runs on the kitchen’s tick and only passes lights that are on, since apply_lighting turns on everything it’s given. Turning the room on and off is left to you.

22.title: Sending the commands yourself
22.content: If you want to send light.turn_on yourself and still have FLARE leave hand-set lights alone: . | flare.claims_check to find out whether someone else has changed the light. | flare.claims_record with what you’re about to send, so FLARE recognises it next time. | Your own light.turn_on. | . For example, this script sets the porch light to a warm 60%, unless someone has changed it since the script last set it: . alias: Porch light warm sequence: - action: flare.claims_check data: entities: [light.porch] response_variable: check - condition: template value_template: "{{ not check.results['light.porch'].blocked }}" - action: flare.claims_record data: entities: [light.porch] room_id: "{{ this.entity_id }}" targets: light.porch: { brightness: 153, color_temp_kelvin: 2200 } - action: light.turn_on target: entity_id: light.porch data: brightness: 153 color_temp_kelvin: 2200 . targets needs the brightness and either color_temp_kelvin or rgb_color you’re sending. FLARE checks the light against it later, so a light running an effect that keeps changing its colour won’t be recognised. For that, use a scene or hand the light over with a null brightness in the blueprint instead. To turn lights off, use flare.turn_off rather than light.turn_off: it records the turn-off too, so it isn’t mistaken for someone switching the lights off by hand. flare.compute_lighting_groups gives you what apply_lighting would send, grouped, without sending it, if you want a starting point for sending it yourself.

23.title: Dashboard
23.content: FLARE comes with a ready-made dashboard: a view for each schedule, and one for your rooms. It builds itself from your schedules and rooms each time it loads, so one you add later appears on its own. Add it from Settings → Dashboards → Add dashboard: pick FLARE Lighting, then give it a name and an icon. FLARE’s logo is in the icon picker as flare:logo. | A schedule’s view shows the day’s curve and every schedule and curve setting. | Overrides starts with All lights: how many lights FLARE is driving across the house, how many something else has taken over, and Clear all to hand every light back at once. Below that is each area with lights a room automation drives, by floor, laid out like Home Assistant’s Lights dashboard: a list of the area’s lights, overridden ones first, headed by its controlled and overridden counts and Clear all to hand them back. Each light shows its status, what FLARE last asked it for and what it’s showing, with its own Clear; press its name to open the light. An area’s name opens its page. Beside the areas, Activity lists the last 24 hours of what the rooms did, coloured by kind - blue when a room takes its lights, amber when something else overrides one, grey when a room lets them go - and the buttons at its top show one kind at a time. On a narrow screen, Activity is a separate tab. | .

24.title: Adding the views to another dashboard
24.content: The same views can go in a dashboard of your own. Open it, then Edit dashboard → the three-dot menu → Raw configuration editor, and add: . views: - title: Lighting strategy: type: custom:flare-schedule - title: Overrides strategy: type: custom:flare-lights . Like the ready-made dashboard, both views find their own entities each time they load. custom:flare-schedule shows every schedule, one after another. To give each schedule its own view instead, add sensor:: . views: - title: Downstairs strategy: type: custom:flare-schedule sensor: downstairs - title: Upstairs strategy: type: custom:flare-schedule sensor: upstairs . sensor is the part before _flare in the schedule sensor’s entity ID, such as downstairs for sensor.downstairs_flare, or the full entity ID, which is what to use if you’ve renamed it. If you name one that doesn’t exist, the view says so and lists the schedules you do have.

25.title: Just the chart
25.content: To put the curve chart on a dashboard of your own: on Home Assistant 2026.6 or newer, add a card, open the By entity tab and pick your schedule sensor — FLARE Curve appears under Community with a preview. On older versions, add a Manual card: . type: custom:flare-curve-card sensor: home . sensor is the part before _flare in the schedule sensor’s entity ID, or the full entity ID, which is what to use if you’ve renamed it.

26.title: Reading a schedule’s view
26.content: Twenty-five near-identical controls is a lot to scan, so two things are colour-coded: . | Colour is the phase — Morning blue, Day amber, Evening deep orange, Night indigo, wherever that phase appears. | Icon is the channel — brightness, colour temperature, or an hourglass for transitions. | . Each Curve row is a colour temperature and a brightness, in that order, and together they preview what the light will look like: both sliders are painted in the colour that phase sets, and how far the brightness one fills is how bright it will be. It’s the same idea as Home Assistant’s own brightness slider for a light. Copy or paste, at the bottom of each schedule, copies that schedule as text, or applies one you paste in, so a schedule can be backed up, shared, or copied onto another. See copying a schedule.

27.title: Changing it
27.content: If you’d rather own the layout and edit it by hand, use Take control from the dashboard’s three-dot menu. Take control is one-way. Once you’ve taken control, the dashboard no longer rebuilds itself, so it won’t pick up changes to FLARE’s layout, and schedules or rooms you add later won’t appear on their own.

28.title: The event loop
28.content: Part of Architecture, for contributors and the curious. Nothing here is needed to use FLARE. Home Assistant runs one asyncio event loop, and nearly everything FLARE does happens on it, as a reaction to something: a state change, a timer, a service call, a registry update. This page lists every hook and explains the rules they follow.

29.title: Callbacks and coroutines
29.content: Home Assistant code comes in three shapes, and getting the shape wrong fails silently until a real event loop runs it. | Shape | Marked | Runs | FLARE uses it for | . | callback | @callback def | on the loop, to completion, no awaiting | listeners, timers, the claim registry’s writers | . | coroutine | async def | on the loop, yielding at each await | service handlers, setup, anything that calls a service | . | plain function | neither | in the executor (a worker thread) | only file and hashing work, through async_add_executor_job | . A listener or timer handed a plain function that touches hass runs it in a worker thread, where hass.async_create_task raises. That’s lesson 7 in CLAUDE.md, and it’s why every listener here carries @callback. Check core.py’s get_hassjob_callable_job_type before trusting a fix in this area: unit tests don’t catch it. Atomic by construction. A callback can’t be interrupted, so anything done inside one is one step as far as the rest of HA is concerned. The claim registry’s writers (async_record, async_override, async_clear, adopt) are callbacks for this reason. In apply_lighting there’s no await between planning the writes and recording their claims, so no state change can land in between and be misjudged. (The async_ prefix is HA’s convention for “must run on the loop”, not “is a coroutine”.) .

30.title: Startup
30.content: sequenceDiagram autonumber participant HA as Home Assistant participant I as flare/__init__.py participant SE as Schedules entry participant ST as Settings entry participant FE as Flares entry HA->>I: async_setup (once per domain) Note over I: static path /flare_static/#lt;hash#gt;/,<br/>add_extra_js_url(loader),<br/>OldFingerprintView, FrontendLoadedView,<br/>export/import_schedule, resolve_target HA->>SE: async_setup_entry Note over SE: a ScheduleCoordinator per schedule,<br/>first refresh (defaults),<br/>forward 6 platforms,<br/>refresh again (restored values) HA->>ST: async_setup_entry Note over ST: ClaimRegistry.async_load (Store),<br/>claimed-light listeners,<br/>blueprint check at started,<br/>9 services, TickScheduler,<br/>forward sensor + button,<br/>release rooms restored dark,<br/>start area ticks HA->>FE: async_setup_entry Note over FE: forward light only if it has flares HA-->>HA: automations load (after integrations) HA-->>FE: EVENT_HOMEASSISTANT_STARTED:<br/>each flare resolves its members HA-->>ST: async_at_started:<br/>check the blueprint . The order inside the Settings entry matters. | Claims load before the platforms, so the sensors start with them. | The services are registered before any platform, so nothing can call one that isn’t there yet. | The claim events start inside the sensor platform (ClaimEvents.start()). They seed every light’s status on the spot, which also notes the mismatch of a claim restored from before a restart. | Only after that are rooms restored dark released, so the release is announced in Activity. | The blueprint check waits for async_at_started: during setup no automation has loaded, so every blueprint looks unused. | . Flares wait for EVENT_HOMEASSISTANT_STARTED for the same reason: automations load after integrations, so a flare can’t read its automation’s inputs until then.

31.title: Every hook
31.content: Bus listeners . | Listener | Where | Reacts by | . | each claimed light’s state | ClaimRegistry.async_start_listening, re-subscribed as the claimed set changes | dropping a claim when its light goes unavailable, releasing a room gone dark, noting mismatches | . | a light’s own state | each _LightStatusSensor | rewriting its status | . | a flare’s member lights | FlareLight, via async_track_target_selector_state_change_event | recomputing the group’s state | . | area_registry_updated | _tick_areas | handing the ticker the new set of areas | . | each claimed light’s registry entry | ClaimRegistry.async_start_listening, alongside its state listener | moving a claim with a rename; dropping it with a deletion | . | a light’s registry entry | each _LightStatusSensor | following a rename; going with its light when it’s removed | . | an automation’s registry entry | each FlareLight, for its own automation | retracking when it’s renamed or removed | . | automation_reloaded | FlareLight | re-reading the automation’s lights | . | homeassistant_started | FlareLight | first membership, once automations exist | . | homeassistant_stop | Settings entry, ClaimEvents | stopping the ticker and timers | . Timers . | Timer | Interval | Where | . | Area tick | each area once per tick_interval minutes (default 1), tick_gap seconds apart (default 1) | TickScheduler, chaining async_track_point_in_utc_time | . | Schedule refresh | 60 s, plus on demand (debounced, at most 10 s) | ScheduleCoordinator (DataUpdateCoordinator) | . | Claims save | 5 s after a change, and at shutdown | Store.async_delay_save | . | Mismatch recheck | once, 31 s after a light first mismatches | ClaimEvents._recheck_after_grace | . | Controlled announcement | 3 s after a room’s first light is taken | ClaimEvents._controlled_soon | . There’s no polling of claim statuses. Everything that can move a count reaches the state listener: a drop, a light going off, one arriving, a mismatch starting or ending. The 30-second grace is the only change that time makes by itself, and it gets its own recheck. Signals . SIGNAL_CLAIMS_UPDATED (dispatcher) is how the registry tells everything showing claims to redraw: the count sensors, the status sensors, the Clear button’s tracked count, and _LightStatuses, which adds a status sensor the first time a room names a light. flowchart LR W["a write<br/>(async_record, adopt,<br/>override, clear)"] --> N L["state listener:<br/>drop / off / arrive /<br/>mismatch change"] --> N N["ClaimRegistry._notify()"] --> SAVE["Store.async_delay_save (5 s)"] N --> EV["ClaimEvents.async_claims_changed()<br/>→ refresh statuses, fire events"] N --> SIG["dispatcher:<br/>SIGNAL_CLAIMS_UPDATED"] SIG --> CS["count sensors"] SIG --> LS["status sensors"] SIG --> BT["Clear button"] SIG --> NEW["_LightStatuses:<br/>add sensors for new lights"] . ClaimEvents is reached directly, through the ClaimListener protocol, rather than by signal, because it must refresh before the sensors redraw. _notify() calls it first. It’s a protocol so tracking/ needn’t import sensor.py.

32.title: Contexts: telling FLARE’s writes apart
32.content: Every state change in HA carries a Context. A service call made with a context passes it to the entity, and the entity’s next state write carries it. Override protection is built on that. sequenceDiagram participant AU as Room automation run participant SV as flare.apply_lighting participant L as light.turn_on participant B as Bulb entity Note over AU: one Context per run (ctx A) AU->>SV: call (context: ctx A) SV->>SV: record claim: latest = ctx A, target SV->>L: light.turn_on (context: ctx A) L->>B: async_turn_on B-->>B: async_write_ha_state()<br/>new state's context = ctx A Note over B: within 5 s: context matches → "controlled"<br/>later reports: compare values with the target . Four facts shape everything built on contexts: . | One context per automation run. Every call in a run shares it, so context.user_id can’t tell FLARE’s write from another automation’s, but context.id can. | An entity forgets the context 5 seconds after the call. A slow bulb that reports later does so under a fresh context, with the values that were asked for. That’s why every claim also records its target, and a light matching the target by value counts as FLARE’s. | Two-step writes make child contexts. Brightness and colour go out as separate calls, each with its own Context(parent_id=...), created before the claims are recorded so both ids are in the claim. | A restart gives every light a new context. Restored claims can only ever match by value. | .

33.title: Ordering subtleties
33.content: . | The Phase event fires after the sensor updates. One coordinator refresh updates the schedule sensor and the Phase event entity. The event entity defers its fire with loop.call_soon, so an automation woken by it reads the sensor’s new phase, not the old one. That’s needed: HA starts the automation’s run inside the event entity’s own state write, so its variables: render before anything after it. | variables: render once, at trigger time. Nothing in the blueprint’s action: may delay, or later steps would act on a stale snapshot (see The room automation). | Claims are recorded before the write. A run cancelled part-way (mode: restart, a two-step bulb mid-sleep) still leaves the claim. A claim for a write that never lands does no harm: the light still matches its previous claim. | .

34.title: Shutdown
34.content: . | Nothing a light reports while HA is stopping counts (hass.is_stopping). MQTT marks its lights unavailable as its connection closes, which would otherwise drop every claim just before the Store’s final write. | The Store writes once more at EVENT_HOMEASSISTANT_FINAL_WRITE, so a clean restart loses nothing. A crash loses at most the last 5 seconds, and FLARE fails open: a light without a claim is free to drive. | The ticker and ClaimEvents cancel their own timers on homeassistant_stop. Nothing unloads config entries at shutdown, and the tests fail on lingering timers. | .

35.title: Examples
35.content: Almost everything in FLARE is an ordinary Home Assistant entity or event. That means you can trigger your own automations from it, or use automations to change it. These are starting points: each one is a complete automation to paste in and adjust. They use a schedule called Home, so its entities are time.home_…, number.home_… and sensor.home_flare. Swap in your own schedule’s name, and your own rooms, lights and sensors. On this page . | A weekend lie-in | A holiday schedule | Movie night | Lighting a room from a remote | Lamps that follow a wall switch | Something else at a phase change | Being told when a light is taken over | .

36.title: A weekend lie-in
36.content: Morning starts later on Saturday and Sunday. alias: Weekend lie-in triggers: - trigger: state entity_id: event.home_flare_phase conditions: - condition: template value_template: "{{ trigger.to_state.attributes.event_type == 'Night' }}" actions: # Friday and Saturday nights set up a lie-in for the next morning; # every other night sets the weekday times back. - variables: lie_in: "{{ now().weekday() in [4, 5] }}" - action: time.set_value target: entity_id: time.home_morning_time data: time: "{{ '08:00:00' if lie_in else '06:00:00' }}" - action: time.set_value target: entity_id: time.home_day_time data: time: "{{ '09:30:00' if lie_in else '08:00:00' }}" . The schedule only checks Morning’s start time when the morning comes round, so the trick is to change it the night before. This runs when Night starts: after today’s morning, and before tomorrow’s. | It runs every night, not just at the weekend, so the weekday times come back on Sunday night without a second automation. | Day moves with Morning. Morning lasts until Day starts, so moving Morning to 08:00 while Day still starts at 08:00 would leave no Morning at all. | If your Night starts after midnight, use [5, 6]: by then it’s already Saturday. | .

37.title: A holiday schedule
37.content: Switch the whole house to a holiday schedule, with later mornings and later nights, from a toggle, and back again when the holiday’s over. First create a Toggle helper called Holiday mode (Settings → Devices & Services → Helpers → Create helper → Toggle). Then: . alias: Holiday schedule triggers: - trigger: state entity_id: input_boolean.holiday_mode actions: - if: "{{ is_state('input_boolean.holiday_mode', 'on') }}" then: - action: flare.import_schedule data: schedule_device_id: "{{ device_id('sensor.home_flare') }}" schedule: | morning: time: "08:30" day: time: "10:00" night: time: "23:30" else: - action: flare.import_schedule data: schedule_device_id: "{{ device_id('sensor.home_flare') }}" schedule: | morning: time: "06:00" day: time: "08:00" night: time: "22:00" . Each schedule lists only what changes; everything else stays as it is. A schedule can hold any of its settings, so for bigger changes, set your schedule up the way you want it, press Copy in its dashboard section, and paste the result in.

38.title: Movie night
38.content: Hold the house at Night while the TV is on, and hand back to the schedule when it goes off. alias: Movie night triggers: - trigger: state entity_id: media_player.living_room_tv to: playing id: start - trigger: state entity_id: media_player.living_room_tv from: playing id: stop actions: - action: select.select_option target: entity_id: select.home_flare_phase data: option: "{{ 'Night' if trigger.id == 'start' else 'Auto' }}" . The phase override applies to every room on that schedule. To dim one room only, give it a schedule of its own, or use the blueprint’s Brightness Template instead.

39.title: Lighting a room from a remote
39.content: Turn the hall lights on from a button on a remote, at the right level for the time of day. alias: Hall lights from the remote triggers: - trigger: state entity_id: event.hall_remote_action conditions: - condition: template value_template: "{{ trigger.to_state.attributes.event_type == 'on' }}" actions: - action: automation.trigger target: entity_id: automation.hallway_lights . If the hall has a flare, you can turn that on instead, like any other light. It runs the room’s automation in the same way: . actions: - action: light.turn_on target: entity_id: light.hallway_lights_flare .

40.title: Lamps that follow a wall switch
40.content: The living room has smart bulbs in its pendants, on an ordinary wall switch, and smart lamps around the room. Switching the pendants off at the wall cuts their power, so Home Assistant sees them go unavailable rather than off. Switching on needs nothing extra. When you switch the pendants on at the wall, they come back online lit, so the room counts as in use and FLARE sets the pendants to the curve and turns the lamps on with them. Switching off needs an automation of its own, because FLARE doesn’t turn the lamps off when the pendants lose power: . alias: Living room lamps off with the pendants triggers: - trigger: state entity_id: - light.living_room_pendant_1 - light.living_room_pendant_2 to: unavailable actions: - action: flare.turn_off data: entities: - light.living_room_lamp_1 - light.living_room_lamp_2 . flare.turn_off turns the lamps off even if you’ve dimmed one yourself. If you’d rather leave the lamps to another automation or a voice assistant, so FLARE never switches them on or off, hand them over with a null level, as in Leaving a light to another automation.

41.title: Something else at a phase change
41.content: Close the blinds when Night starts. alias: Blinds at Night triggers: - trigger: state entity_id: event.home_flare_phase conditions: - condition: template value_template: "{{ trigger.to_state.attributes.event_type == 'Night' }}" actions: - action: cover.close_cover target: area_id: living_room . The Phase event fires each time the phase changes, including a manual override, with the new phase as its event_type.

42.title: Being told when a light is taken over
42.content: A notification when FLARE stops driving a light because something else changed it. alias: Tell me when FLARE lets go of a light triggers: - trigger: event event_type: flare_light_overridden actions: - action: notify.notify data: message: > {{ state_attr(trigger.event.data.light, 'friendly_name') }} was changed by something else, so FLARE has stopped driving it until the room goes dark. The event also carries what FLARE last asked for and what the light was actually showing — see FLARE’s events.

43.title: Flares
43.content: A flare is a light entity that sits over an automation. Flares are under Settings → Devices & Services → FLARE → Flares. For setting one up for a voice assistant, see Voice assistants and HomeKit. On this page . | Settings | The flare’s light | Flares and the room’s automation | .

44.title: Settings
44.content: | Setting | Description | . | Automation | The automation that turning the flare on runs. If the automation is deleted, the flare is unavailable. | . | Lights input | For an automation built from a blueprint: the input that holds the lights. The flare reads it whenever it’s used, so a change to the automation changes the flare. For an automation from the FLARE blueprint this is Lights & Occupancy. | . | Lights | For an automation not built from a blueprint: the lights, picked directly. | . | Area | Only when adding: the area the flare’s device starts in, which defaults to the automation’s area. After that, the device’s area is set the usual way. | . Set up area offers a flare for each area it sets up, named after the area. Adding flares from Rooms from the FLARE blueprint creates one for each room picked, named after its automation. Either way, the flare starts in the automation’s area. Reconfigure shows which automation the flare runs, and changes the flare’s name and its lights, or its lights input. It can’t change the automation, so to use a different one, add a new flare.

45.title: The flare’s light
45.content: light.<name>_flare reports the combined state of its lights, as a Home Assistant light group does: on if any of them is on, with their average brightness and colour. Its entity_id attribute lists the lights. | Call | What it does | . | light.turn_on with no brightness, colour or effect | Runs the automation, as Run actions does. A transition on its own is ignored. | . | light.turn_on with a brightness, colour or effect | Marks every light as overridden, with the automation as its room, with flare.claims_override, then sends the values to them, as a light group does. FLARE leaves them alone until the room is empty and dark. | . | light.turn_off | Marks every light as overridden in the same way, then turns them off. They stay off until the room’s automation next turns them on, such as when it detects motion. | . The flare’s lights are the same as its automation’s, chosen as described under Room. A light that belongs to another flare isn’t one of them.

46.title: Flares and the room’s automation
46.content: A flare’s own light is never one of a room’s lights: the FLARE blueprint and FLARE’s services skip it, even when it sits in the room’s area.

47.title: How flares work
47.content: Part of Architecture, for contributors and the curious. Nothing here is needed to use FLARE. A flare (light.<name>_flare) is a light that fronts a room automation, so a voice assistant, HomeKit or a dashboard can switch a room without going around it. Saying “turn the kitchen on” to Siri goes to the flare, and the flare runs the kitchen’s automation. Siri’s own “on” sent straight to the bulbs would read as an override, and the room would be left at whatever the bulbs restored to.

48.title: What it is in code
48.content: FlareLight (light.py) subclasses HA’s own LightGroup, so state, brightness and colour are the group’s, worked out from its members. Two things differ from a plain light group: who its members are, and what “on” means. flowchart LR sub["Flares entry subentry<br/>{automation: registry id,<br/>lights_input: room_target}"] --> inst["FlareInstance"] inst --> fl["FlareLight<br/>(LightGroup)"] auto["automation entity<br/>_blueprint_inputs"] -->|"lights_target()"| tgt["target<br/>{area_id: kitchen}"] tgt -->|"async_track_target_selector_<br/>state_change_event"| mem["members:<br/>the room's lights, minus flares"] mem --> fl . Membership . A flare stores two things: its automation, by entity-registry id so a rename doesn’t orphan it, and the name of the input holding the room’s lights (room_target for our blueprint). It reads the input’s value live. A plain automation, not made from a blueprint, stores a target instead. | The inputs come from the automation entity’s private _blueprint_inputs (flares/automation.py:blueprint_inputs). Its raw_config is the substituted config, so it doesn’t have them. This is an accepted risk, kept to that one function, and the behaviour tests break if HA changes it. | Members are tracked with async_track_target_selector_state_change_event, HA’s own target resolution: the same rule as flare.resolve_target, so a flare’s members are exactly its room’s lights. | It re-resolves on automation_reloaded, on entity-registry changes to automations, and once at homeassistant_started (automations load after integrations). | A flare is never one of a room’s lights. The room’s tick would send it the curve, and the flare would pass that on to every bulb as an override. Three layers stop it: the blueprint rejects integration_entities('flare'), the services drop flare lights (flares/identity.without_flares), and a flare’s own member filter drops other flares. Without the last, a flare could contain itself and recurse forever. | . On and off . flowchart TB on["light.turn_on on the flare"] --> bare{"bare?<br/>(no keys but transition)"} bare -->|"yes"| trig["automation.trigger<br/>→ manual run: allow_turn_on, force"] bare -->|"no, values given"| mark1["flare.claims_override(members, room)"] mark1 --> grp1["LightGroup.turn_on(values)"] off["light.turn_off on the flare"] --> mark2["flare.claims_override(members, room)"] mark2 --> grp2["LightGroup.turn_off<br/>(a plain light.turn_off)"] . | A bare “on” runs the automation. How a room comes on is the automation’s decision. A manual run passes allow_turn_on and force, so “on” also takes back a room that was overridden. | “On” with values, and “off”, mark the lights overridden first, with the automation as the room, then send as any light group does. Without that, an unclaimed light (every light, once a room goes dark) would read untracked, and the run the change itself triggers would take it straight back to the curve. That’s how Siri’s “100 %” got dimmed back down. The override claim has a fresh context and no target, so it never matches; the room going dark hands the lights back. | Off is a plain light.turn_off, never flare.turn_off. A flare’s off is the user’s. Recording it as FLARE’s off would let a run landing while the room was half-off switch it back on. | . It reaches flare.claims_override as a service call because that’s the Settings entry’s, which may not be loaded. has_service checks first.

49.title: The light platform only loads with flares
49.content: The Flares entry forwards the light platform only when it has at least one flare, and remembers whether it did in entry.runtime_data so unload matches. An empty entry has nothing to put on it, and setting light up that early interfered with the behaviour tests’ fake bulbs.

50.title: Adding flares
50.content: . | Add Flare lists only automations made from our blueprint. Any other automation goes through a custom path offering only inputs that can hold lights (lights_input_kinds). | Area setup adds them in bulk, one subentry each, and the entry’s update listener coalesces the reloads into one (_async_reload_entry). | Nothing creates a flare on its own except area setup, where the user ticks the rooms. A HomeKit bridge including light, or a voice assistant exposing new entities, would otherwise put every room in the Home app after an update. | A new flare’s device goes in its automation’s area once, at creation (_place_in_area). After that, the area is the user’s. | .

51.title: Voice assistants and HomeKit
51.content: A flare is a light for a whole room. Turning it on runs the room’s automation, so “Hey Siri, turn on the kitchen” brings the kitchen up the way FLARE would have, at the curve’s brightness and colour, rather than at whatever the bulbs last had. On this page . | Adding flares for your rooms . | Name it the way you’ll say it | . | What each command does | Exposing flares instead of your bulbs . | HomeKit | Alexa and Google Assistant | Assist | . | A flare for your own automation | .

52.title: Adding flares for your rooms
52.content: After setting up areas with Set up area, including when you first add FLARE, choose Pick rooms for flares. Every room you just set up is listed and ticked, and each one you keep gets a flare named after its area. For a room automation you made yourself, go to Settings → Devices & Services → FLARE → Add flare and choose Rooms from the FLARE blueprint. Every room automation that doesn’t have a flare yet is listed and ticked, so you can add a flare for every room at once, or untick the ones you don’t want. Each one is named after its automation. A flare is placed in its automation’s area. It appears as light.<name>_flare and always has the same lights as its room’s automation, so if you add a bulb to the room’s area, it joins the flare too. Name it the way you’ll say it . A flare’s name is what Siri, Alexa and Google hear. Automations often have names like “Kitchen lighting” or “Garden Lights Adaptive”, which nobody says out loud, so rename a flare named after one to the room’s plain name, “Kitchen” or “Garden”, with Reconfigure in the flare’s three-dot menu. Renaming a flare doesn’t change its entity ID. If the flare is already in the Home app or the Alexa app, rename it there too, because they can keep the name they first saw.

53.title: What each command does
53.content: | You say or tap | What happens | . | “Turn on the kitchen” | The room’s automation runs, and the room comes on the way it normally would. | . | “Set the kitchen to 30%”, or a colour | Every light in the room is set to that. FLARE leaves them there until the room is empty and dark. | . | “Turn on the kitchen” again | The room goes back to FLARE: the automation runs, and every light returns to the curve. | . | “Turn off the kitchen” | Every light in the room turns off, and stays off until the room’s sensors next detect motion. | .

54.title: Exposing flares instead of your bulbs
54.content: Expose each room’s flare and stop exposing its bulbs. If you expose both, every room shows up twice, and “turn on the kitchen” may go to the bulbs, which come on at whatever they last had instead of following the room. The bulbs keep working in Home Assistant either way. HomeKit . FLARE names every flare light.<name>_flare, so if your HomeKit Bridge is set up in YAML, one pattern exports every flare, including ones you add later: . homekit: filter: include_entity_globs: - light.*_flare . Leave out include_domains: light if you have it, or the bulbs are exported as well. Home Assistant reads this when it starts, so restart after changing it. If you set the bridge up from the UI instead, use Configure on the HomeKit Bridge integration, choose to include entities, and pick the flares. HomeKit doesn’t use Home Assistant’s areas, so put each flare in its room in the Home app. If the bridge used to export your bulbs, they stay in the Home app as “Not Responding” until you remove the bridge from the Home app and pair it again. Alexa and Google Assistant . With Home Assistant Cloud, go to Settings → Voice assistants → Expose, expose the flares and un-expose the bulbs. If Expose new entities is on, the flares are already exposed, but so is every bulb. Google Assistant puts each flare in the room matching its Home Assistant area. Alexa doesn’t use areas, so put each flare in a group for its room in the Alexa app. If you set up exposure in YAML instead, the same include_entity_globs pattern works in the filter: under cloud: alexa:, cloud: google_actions: and a manual alexa: smart_home:. A manual google_assistant: setup has no filter, so expose the flares there with entity_config instead. Assist . Assist uses the same Expose list. Expose the flares and un-expose the bulbs, and “turn on the kitchen” turns on the flare. If you’d rather keep the flare’s name as it is, add the room’s name as an alias on the flare instead, under Voice assistants in its settings.

55.title: A flare for your own automation
55.content: Any automation can have a flare. Choose Another automation when adding one: . | If the automation is built from a blueprint, pick the input that holds its lights. | A brightness or colour you set from the flare is only protected if the automation passes itself as its room, room_id: "{{ this.entity_id }}". Otherwise, if FLARE wasn’t already driving a light, the automation’s next update can set it back. | If it isn’t, pick its lights directly. | . Turning the flare on runs that automation. The other commands work the same as above. The Flares reference lists every setting.

56.title: Dashboard internals
56.content: Part of Architecture, for contributors and the curious. Nothing here is needed to use FLARE. The dashboard is plain JavaScript modules in custom_components/flare/www/, served by the integration itself. There’s no build step and no dependency. It’s made of Lovelace strategies, which generate the dashboard’s config on every load, plus a handful of custom cards and card features.

57.title: Getting into the page
57.content: sequenceDiagram autonumber participant B as Browser participant HA as HA http participant L as flare-loader.js participant M as FLARE modules Note over HA: async_setup:<br/>static path /flare_static/#lt;hash#gt;/ → www/,<br/>add_extra_js_url(loader) B->>HA: GET / (page HTML lists extra modules) B->>HA: GET /flare_static/#lt;hash#gt;/flare-loader.js HA-->>B: the loader (cached hard) B->>L: run L->>L: await customElements.whenDefined('home-assistant') L->>M: import icon, curve card, features,<br/>transfer card, view strategy M-->>B: customElements.define,<br/>window.customStrategies / customCards /<br/>customCardFeatures / customIcons L->>HA: import /flare_static/frontend_loaded.js Note over HA: the beacon: clears the<br/>"reload for dashboard" repair . The fingerprint. The static path carries a hash of every file under www/ (www_fingerprint()), and is served with long-lived cache headers. Any change to any file is a new URL. A version number wasn’t enough: a dev build is always 0.0.0-dev, and Safari kept serving a stale strategy. | It’s a path segment, not ?v=. The modules import each other relatively, and a relative import inherits the path but not a query, so ?v= would load a module twice and the second customElements.define would throw. test_static_imports.py pins relative imports. | Any other fingerprint redirects (302) to the current one (OldFingerprintView). A page served before an update, such as the service worker’s stale copy or the companion app, still asks for the old hash, and a 404 would mean no dashboard at all. | . Waiting for <home-assistant>. As it boots, HA’s frontend installs a scoped custom-element registry polyfill, replacing window.customElements, while it loads integrations’ modules in parallel. A module that defined its elements first put them in the browser’s own registry, where HA never looks. The dashboard was then listed but timed out when picked. The frontend reads extra modules only from the page HTML at load time, so a page open while FLARE is set up never gets them. On HTTPS or localhost, the service worker serves the first reload from its stale cache too. dashboard_reload.py handles both: setup’s summary and a repair link to a reload with a one-off query token, a URL the service worker has never cached, with target="_self" so it’s a real page load. 71.title: What it does
71.content: FLARE sets your lights through the day, and leaves alone any light you change yourself. | It lights the room when you walk in. With a motion or occupancy sensor, the room comes on at the right brightness and colour for the time of day, or in the scene you’ve picked for it, and turns off once it’s empty. | It works with lights on a physical wall switch. If you cut the power to a room and restore it, FLARE puts each bulb on the current phase as soon as it shows up in Home Assistant again, instead of leaving it at whatever it powered up as. | It keeps every light on the curve. Every minute it checks each light, and corrects any that have drifted or missed a command. | Each room can be different. Give a light its own brightness, hand the room to a scene in any phase, or use a template when a fixed value isn’t enough. | It can leave a nightlight on. When a room empties it can dim to a low level instead of going dark. | It leaves your changes alone. If you change a light yourself, from an app, a wall switch or another automation, FLARE stops setting it until the room next goes dark. | It works with Siri, Alexa and Google. Each room gets a single light to expose to them, so “turn on the kitchen” lights the kitchen the way FLARE would, rather than at whatever the bulbs were last set to. If you ask for a brightness or colour, FLARE leaves it alone. | It’s gentle on your Zigbee network. Rooms update one after another rather than all at once, and changes too small to see aren’t sent. | .

72.title: Setting it up
72.content: Adding FLARE sets up every room with lights, then the dashboard. The Quickstart goes through it step by step.

73.title: Four phases, not one curve
73.content: Most adaptive lighting follows the sun’s position. That means evening lighting at 4pm in winter, and bright light until 9pm in summer, whatever time you actually get up and go to bed. FLARE works from your schedule instead, dividing the day into four named phases. With the default settings: . | Phase | What it’s for | . | Morning | Bright and cold — enough eyeball caffeine to get you as far as the coffee machine, with some research to back it up. | . | Day | Bright, easing steadily from Morning’s colour toward Evening’s across the whole afternoon. | . | Evening | Dimming and warming, anchored to your actual sunset. | . | Night | Warm and low, flat until morning. | . Each boundary has its own transition: how long beforehand to start easing into the next phase, so the new values land exactly as it begins. If you set a transition to zero, the lights step straight to the new values instead. Morning, Day and Night start at fixed times of day. Only Evening tracks the sun, and it’s kept between an earliest and a latest time, so it moves with the season without drifting into the small hours. Play with the curve to see how each setting shapes the day.
