90.title: How it works
90.content: When flare.apply_lighting or flare.turn_off changes a light, it records a claim on the light. On the next update, FLARE compares the light with its claim. If the light still shows what FLARE set, FLARE carries on setting it. If it doesn’t, something else has changed it, and FLARE leaves it alone. Claims are FLARE’s, not any one automation’s: a light one automation set is FLARE’s to every other automation too. A light that’s on, has no claim, and already shows what flare.apply_lighting would set isn’t changed, so FLARE claims it as it is. After a Clear, for example, a room’s lights are claimed again on their next update even if none of them needs changing. Rooms . Each call that records claims names a room, usually the automation making it, and the room’s lights. The blueprint passes its own automation as room_id and its Lights & Occupancy lights as room_entities. If you call the services yourself, do the same: . action: flare.apply_lighting data: entities: [light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2] brightness: 200 color_temp_kelvin: 3200 transition: 2 room_id: "{{ this.entity_id }}" room_entities: [light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2, light.kitchen_lamp] . | Without room_id, apply_lighting, turn_off and compute_lighting_groups set the lights but record nothing, and don’t leave any light alone. | claims_record and claims_override require room_id. claims_check and claims_clear don’t take one. | Without room_entities, a room’s lights are the ones its calls have set. | force: true sets lights even if something else has changed them, and records the claim. | A light FLARE has no claim on is free for FLARE to set, so a change your own automation makes to one isn’t left alone unless you mark it with flare.claims_override. | . If an automation is renamed, its room carries on: FLARE keeps rooms by the automation’s entity registry entry, not its entity ID. The two claims . Each tracked light has two claims: . | latest: the last change FLARE sent to the light. | observed: a change FLARE has seen the light report. On its next update, if the light reports latest’s context, FLARE promotes latest to observed. | . A light matching either claim is FLARE’s. So a change that never reaches the light, such as a dropped Zigbee command, doesn’t make FLARE treat the light as changed by someone else; the light still matches observed. A light matches a claim if it reports the context of that claim’s change, or the values in it. Values are needed because Home Assistant drops a change’s context after five seconds, and some bulbs take longer than that to report back. How close counts as a match . A light matches a claim’s values if it’s within a tolerance of them, so only a change you’d notice counts as someone else’s. Bulbs rarely report back exactly what they were sent: a colour temperature asked for as 4294 K can come back as 4312 K. You can set the tolerances under FLARE → Settings → Configure: . | Option | Default | Description | . | Brightness tolerance | 5% | How far, as a percentage of the brightness FLARE asked for, a light’s brightness can be and still match. A dim light always gets at least 2 (of 255). | . | Colour temperature tolerance | 5 mireds | How far a light’s colour temperature can be from what FLARE asked for and still match. For a light FLARE sets by RGB, the red, green and blue differences added together can be up to twice this (10 by default). | . The same tolerances decide what’s worth sending: a light that close to its target isn’t sent anything. If lights are marked overridden when nobody has changed them, raise the one that matches the difference shown on the dashboard. Lower them to catch smaller changes. Claims are kept across a restart. After a restart every light has a new context, so restored claims are matched by values only: a light still showing what FLARE set is FLARE’s, and any other light is left alone. Turning a light off counts . Turning a light off yourself counts as changing it, so FLARE doesn’t turn it back on. FLARE’s own turn-offs record a claim of {"state": "off"}, which is how FLARE tells them apart from yours. When FLARE sets a light again . A room discards its claims when none of its claimed lights are on. This is what normally ends an override: once the room is dark, FLARE sets every light in it again. | A light FLARE has no claim on doesn’t count, so a lamp in the room that something else runs can’t keep the room’s claims. | A light that’s unavailable counts as off, so one dead bulb can’t either. | After a restart, a room whose claimed lights are all off once they’ve reported in discards its claims too, so a room switched off while Home Assistant was restarting comes on again as usual. | A light in two rooms loses its claim when either of them goes dark. | . A light also loses its claim when it goes unavailable, and you can discard claims by hand with Clear, the dashboard’s Clear for an area, or flare.claims_clear. A light that has just come back online, say switched on at the wall, starts at whatever it powers up as, and misses a command sent while it boots. So when a room’s lights come back online together, FLARE waits a few seconds before setting them.

91.title: FLARE’s events
91.content: FLARE says when a room takes its lights, when it lets them go, and when something else changes one of them. Each event is filed under one of FLARE’s entities (its Controlled or Overridden count, or Clear for a release) and FLARE’s device, so they appear in its Activity. room names the automation. FLARE adjusting lights it already has isn’t announced. When a room starts controlling lights it wasn’t, such as when it comes on, FLARE fires flare_lights_controlled once for them all, a few seconds after the first, since the bulbs report back one by one: . lights: [light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2] # the lights it took controlled: 6 # how many of its lights FLARE is controlling now room: automation.kitchen_lighting entity_id: sensor.flare_controlled_lights device_id: ... # FLARE's device . Controlled lights Kitchen Lighting is now controlling 6 lights . When a room lets its lights go, because it went dark or you pressed Clear, FLARE fires flare_lights_released: . lights: [light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2] room: automation.kitchen_lighting entity_id: button.flare_clear device_id: ... Clear Kitchen Lighting cleared 6 lights . When something else changes one of FLARE’s lights, and it stays changed for 30 seconds, FLARE fires flare_light_overridden for that light: . light: light.kitchen_1 rooms: [automation.kitchen_lighting] # every room it's one of entity_id: sensor.flare_overridden_lights device_id: ... previous_status: controlled live_context_id: 01M11... live: { state: on, brightness: 12, color_temp_kelvin: 6500 } # or rgb_color, for a colour observed: { context_id: ..., target: {...}, recorded_at: ... } latest: { context_id: ..., target: {...}, recorded_at: ... } . Overridden lights Kitchen Lighting released Kitchen 1 to something else (last asked for 255/6667, found 12/6500) . live is what the light was showing: its brightness and colour temperature, or its rgb_color if it wasn’t showing a white. A light reporting its colour as xy that’s showing a white has its colour temperature worked out from it. It fires once when the light changes hands, not again while the light stays overridden, and not for lights that were already overridden before a restart. To trigger an automation on it: . triggers: - trigger: event event_type: flare_light_overridden .

92.title: Inspecting tracked state
92.content: flare.claims_check returns each light’s status, and each light’s status sensor shows it: . | Status | Meaning | . | controlled | FLARE is setting it: it matches one of its claims. | . | overridden | It has matched neither claim for at least 30 seconds, so something else has changed it. | . | mismatched | It has matched neither claim for less than 30 seconds. Usually it’s FLARE’s own change still arriving, or a light just back online reporting late, so it isn’t counted or announced as overridden yet. It’s left alone meanwhile, the same as an overridden light. | . | untracked | It’s on, and has no claim, or only one FLARE hasn’t seen the light report yet. FLARE sets it as usual. | . | off | It’s off and has no claim. A light FLARE turned off is controlled; one someone else turned off is overridden. | . | unavailable | Home Assistant can’t reach it, so its claims aren’t checked. It isn’t blocked. | . matched_via says which claim matched, and how: latest-context, latest-value, observed-context or observed-value. rooms lists the rooms the light is one of. Each claim has a recorded_at time and a context_id, which you can use to find the change in Home Assistant’s logbook. A light’s claim follows it when it’s renamed, and goes when it’s deleted from Home Assistant.

93.title: When rooms update
93.content: FLARE fires a flare_tick event for each area once per update interval, carrying the area as area_id. Areas tick one after another, in name order, a gap apart, so rooms don’t all send commands at the same time. A tick is a plain event, not an entity, so it never appears in Activity, history or the logbook. You can set the interval and the gap under FLARE → Settings → Configure: . | Option | Default | Description | . | Update interval | 1 minute | How often each area ticks, from 1 to 60 minutes. | . | Gap between areas | 1 second | Reduced automatically when the areas wouldn’t otherwise fit in the interval. | . A room automation from the blueprint follows the tick of the first area in its Lights & Occupancy. To run your own automation on an area’s tick: . triggers: - trigger: event event_type: flare_tick event_data: area_id: kitchen .

94.title: Curve playground
94.content: Move any setting and the chart shows the day it makes, exactly as it appears on your dashboard. Four phases, not one curve explains what each phase is for. The chart's height is brightness and its colour is the colour temperature at that moment. The vertical line is "now" — drag Time of day to move it. Defaults Winter sunset Midsummer sunset Late riser Very warm night Copy link to these settings Copy schedule . Time of day . Moves the "now" marker. Nothing about the schedule changes — this is just where you're standing in the day. Time of day Schedule . When each phase begins. Every one of these is a time entity on the schedule you add in Home Assistant — except sunset, which comes from sun.sun. Brightness . Each phase's brightness. Evening's is a starting point rather than a hold: it fades toward Night's value over the run-up to Night Start. Colour temperature . Each phase holds its own colour and eases to the next one over that phase's transition, below. Transitions . How long before each phase ends to start easing toward the next one — so the new phase's values have arrived exactly as it begins. Set one to zero for a deliberate, visible change at that boundary. Anything longer than the phase it runs in simply covers the whole phase, which is why Day's colour transition defaults to a full day: it slides from Morning's colour to Evening's across the entire afternoon. Load a schedule . Paste a schedule copied from Home Assistant (its Copy button on the schedule dashboard, or the schedule's Reconfigure) to see its curve here. Copy schedule above goes the other way: paste the result into Home Assistant to use these settings. Anything a schedule leaves out keeps its value here. Load . |

95.title: The room automation
95.content: Part of Architecture, for contributors and the curious. Nothing here is needed to use FLARE. custom_components/flare/blueprints/flare.yaml is the blueprint each room automation is made from. It decides when a room updates and whether a light may come on. The services decide how: what to send, to which bulbs, and which lights to leave alone.

96.title: Why the split falls where it does
96.content: A condition: can’t call a service. So anything a condition needs has to be a template or a native condition, and that keeps triggers, conditions and occupancy in the blueprint. Anything that needs HA’s registries properly (which lights are the room’s), or is fiddly enough to want unit tests (grouping, override protection), is a service the blueprint calls in its action:. flowchart LR subgraph YAML["Blueprint (Jinja/YAML)"] tr["triggers"] co["the one top-level condition"] va["variables: occupancy, levels,<br/>idle, scenes, allow_turn_on"] ch["choose: off / self-heal / default"] end subgraph PY["Integration (Python)"] rt["flare.resolve_target"] sc["flare.compute_scene_coverage"] al["flare.apply_lighting"] to["flare.turn_off"] cc["flare.claims_clear"] end tr --> co --> rt --> va --> ch ch --> sc ch --> al ch --> to ch --> cc .

97.title: Triggers
97.content: | id | Fires on | Notes | . | phase_change | the schedule’s Phase event entity | a real phase change, and once after setup | . | tick | flare_tick with this room’s tick_area | the curve moves within a phase | . | tick | time_pattern every minute | only when the room names no area, chosen by enabled: | . | extra | Additional Triggers | any state change of entities the user picked | . | motion_on | occupancy.detected, motion.detected | native triggers over room_target | . | motion_off | occupancy.cleared, motion.cleared, held for Wait time | per sensor | . | recovered | template: some room light reachable, held 5 s | all the room’s lights were unreachable and one is back | . | lux_dark | template: the room stops reading too bright (some illuminance sensor at or below Lux Threshold) | a wake-up only; the action re-checks | . trigger_variables: are the only variables a trigger can see. tick_area is computed there, as the first area_id in room_target. Trigger templates are limited: they can’t call area_devices() and friends, so recovered and lux_dark expand room_target by hand in Jinja. That’s close enough for a wake-up. The action works from the real resolution.

98.title: The action, step by step
98.content: flowchart TB start(["a trigger fires"]) --> cond{"top-level condition:<br/>a sensor Sensors From<br/>Areas leaves out?"} cond -->|"yes"| drop(["no run"]) cond -->|"no"| rt["flare.resolve_target(room_target)<br/>→ room.entities"] rt --> vars["variables step:<br/>resolved_entities, levels, idle,<br/>occupancy, allow_turn_on, scenes"] vars --> stop{"motion_on, and nothing<br/>off or idle?"} stop -->|"yes"| s(["stop"]) stop -->|"no"| choose{"choose"} choose -->|"motion_off and every sensor<br/>clear for the Wait time"| off["flare.turn_off(turn_off_entities)<br/>then idle lights dimmed"] choose -->|"tick or phase_change, sensors clear<br/>for the Wait time, something still on"| heal["self-heal:<br/>flare.turn_off(entities_still_on)"] choose -->|"default"| cov["scene chosen?<br/>flare.compute_scene_coverage"] cov --> idle{"room_is_idle?"} idle -->|"yes"| idl["flare.apply_lighting(idle_entities,<br/>idle_levels)"] idle --> gate{"allow_turn_on<br/>and not room_is_idle"} idl --> gate gate -->|"yes"| scene["scene.turn_on, if due<br/>(never on a tick)"] scene --> apply["flare.apply_lighting(target_entities,<br/>curve, levels, force: manual_run)"] gate -->|"no"| release apply --> release["claims_clear for lights handed<br/>to a scene or a null level"] . The variables chain . variables: render top to bottom, once, when the run starts, and an undefined name fails silently (x | length is 0). So order matters, and the chain reads like this: . flowchart LR room["room.entities"] --> res["resolved_entities<br/>(lights, minus flares)"] room --> occ["room_occupancy_entities<br/>(working sensors)"] room --> lux["room_lux_entities"] --> tb["too_bright"] --> lb["lux_blocked_entities"] res --> bl["brightness_levels<br/>(exclude lists + template)"] --> ho["hands_off_entities<br/>(null / false)"] res --> ib["idle_brightness"] --> ie["idle_entities"] ho --> ie lb --> ie occ --> ocw["occupancy_clear_for_wait"] ie --> idle["room_is_idle"] occ --> idle ocw --> idle res --> occd["occupied<br/>(any light on)"] occd --> atl["allow_turn_on"] ocw --> atl tb --> atl . The gate . Exactly two things can switch a light on, scene.turn_on and flare.apply_lighting, and both sit inside one if allow_turn_on block in default:. allow_turn_on = manual_run or trigger.id == 'motion_on' or occupied # a light in the room is already on or (trigger.id == 'lux_dark' and not too_bright and someone is in the room) . It must never gain a new way to become true without the user asking for it explicitly. test_no_trigger_reaching_default_can_light_a_dark_empty_room sweeps every trigger against it. The one exception is idle brightness, the nightlight: an empty room settles to its idle levels outside the gate. It’s gated on room_is_idle instead, and the curve’s gate is allow_turn_on and not room_is_idle. Without that, an idle light being on would make occupied true, and the next tick would ramp the nightlight straight back up. Why there’s no delay anywhere in action: . Variables are a snapshot taken when the run starts. A delay before acting would act on that snapshot. A 0–15 s jitter delay once relit a light switched off by hand inside the window, because the run had already decided the room was in use. test_nothing_delays_the_action_before_it_decides pins it. A trigger’s own for: (as recovered and motion_off have) isn’t a delay in this sense, because the run, and so its variables, starts after it.

100.title: Occupancy, briefly
100.content: . | room_occupancy_entities exists only to know whether the room has a sensor at all. occupancy.is_detected over zero entities is vacuously false, so a lights-only room would otherwise always read empty. | An unavailable sensor is left out, so a room whose only sensor is dead counts as sensorless rather than empty. | occupancy_clear_for_wait is a hand-written now() - last_changed check. The native for: needs the recorder to prime it after a restart, and that isn’t reliable. | With Sensors From Areas off, the native triggers still fire for every sensor in the target (a trigger’s target: takes no templates), so the top-level condition: drops the ones not named directly. | A sensor excluded from the target (exclude:, HA 2026.11) never fires the native triggers and isn’t in flare.resolve_target’s entities, so the blueprint needs no code for exclusions. Only the lux_dark and recovered wake-ups ignore them, since their Jinja expands the target itself. | .

101.title: Scenes
101.content: A room can follow a scene of yours instead of the curve: one per phase, or one chosen by a template. FLARE applies the scene, lights anything it doesn’t cover from the curve, and takes the room back when the scene no longer applies. On this page . | Handing a room to a scene | When the scene is applied | .

102.title: Handing a room to a scene
102.content: If you pick a scene in the blueprint’s Night Scene (or whichever phase), the room uses it instead of the curve during that phase. For anything a phase can’t express — a different scene while the TV is on — use Scene Template, which wins over the per-phase pickers whenever it returns a scene. A scene is only used if every entity it touches is in the room. A scene that reaches into another room, or doesn’t exist, is ignored and the room follows the curve. Lights in the room that the scene doesn’t cover carry on following the curve, so a scene naming half the room leaves the other half to FLARE.

103.title: When the scene is applied
103.content: The scene is applied when the room’s automation runs for a phase change, for motion, for an Additional Trigger, when you run it by hand, or when a light comes back online — but not on the regular update. Re-applying it every minute would undo anything you changed by hand while it was on. Like the curve, a scene never lights an empty room. If the phase changes while nobody’s there, the scene is applied when someone next walks in.

104.title: Schedules
104.content: A schedule sets when each of the four phases starts, and the brightness and colour temperature in each phase. Adding FLARE creates your schedules. You can add more, for example for rooms that need different timing, with Settings → Devices & Services → FLARE → Add schedule. On this page . | A schedule’s entities | The schedule sensor | Transitions | Copying a schedule | .

105.content: | Entity | Description | . | sensor.<name>_flare | The current phase, brightness and colour. See the schedule sensor. | . | event.<name>_flare_phase | Fires when the phase changes, including a manual override. The event type is the new phase’s name. | . | select.<name>_flare_phase | Overrides the phase. Auto (the default) follows the schedule; choosing a phase holds it until the schedule reaches its next phase. | . | switch.<name>_sticky_phase_override | When on, an override stays until you set the phase back to Auto. | . | time.<name>_morning_time, day_time, night_time | When Morning, Day and Night start. Defaults: 06:00, 08:00, 22:00. If Night’s time is earlier than Morning’s, such as 01:00, Night starts after midnight, and Evening runs until then. | . | time.<name>_evening_earliest_time, evening_latest_time | Evening starts at sunset, but no earlier or later than these. Defaults: 17:00, 20:00. | . | number.<name>_<phase>_brightness | The phase’s brightness, 0–255. At 0, the phase turns the lights off. | . | number.<name>_<phase>_kelvin | The phase’s colour temperature, 1000–10000 K. | . | number.<name>_<phase>_brightness_transition, _kelvin_transition | The phase’s transitions, in minutes. 106.title: The schedule sensor
106.content: | Attribute | Description | . | state | The phase: Morning, Day, Evening or Night. | . | brightness | The current brightness, 0–255. | . | color_temp | The current colour temperature, in Kelvin. | . | rgb_color | The current colour temperature as [r, g, b]. | . | morning_start, day_start, evening_start, night_start | Today’s phase start times, as timestamps. | . | evening_earliest, evening_latest | Today’s earliest and latest Evening start, as timestamps. | . | points | The whole day as 289 {t, brightness, kelvin} samples, used by the chart. | . The sensor updates every minute. While the phase is overridden, every attribute except points follows the overridden phase.

107.title: Transitions
107.content: A phase’s transition is how long before the phase ends its brightness or colour starts changing to the next phase’s. The change finishes when the next phase starts: if Morning starts at 06:00, the lights reach Morning’s values at 06:00. For example, day_kelvin_transition is how long before the end of Day the colour starts changing to Evening’s. | A transition of 0 switches at the boundary. | A transition longer than its phase covers the whole phase. | . Brightness and colour have separate transitions. By default, Day’s colour transition is 1440 minutes, so its colour changes across the whole of Day, while its brightness changes only in roughly the last hour. Night runs past midnight, so its transition is in the minutes before Morning starts. If Night starts after midnight, Evening runs past midnight instead, and its transition is in the minutes before Night starts.

108.title: Copying a schedule
108.content: A schedule’s settings can be copied as YAML: . morning: time: "06:00" brightness: 255 kelvin: 6667 brightness_transition: 30 kelvin_transition: 30 evening: earliest: "17:00" latest: "20:00" brightness: 180 night: kelvin: 2000 . Each phase takes brightness, kelvin, brightness_transition and kelvin_transition, and a start time. Evening takes earliest and latest instead of time. When you apply a schedule, settings it leaves out keep their current values. To copy or apply a schedule, use any of: . | Copy and Paste at the bottom of each schedule on the dashboard. | Reconfigure in the schedule’s three-dot menu under FLARE → Schedules, which shows the schedule as text that you can replace and submit. | The services flare.export_schedule and flare.import_schedule. | Copy schedule and Load in the curve playground. | . A schedule with an error in it, such as an unknown setting, an invalid time or a value out of range, isn’t applied. The error message says what’s wrong.

109.title: Schedules and the curve
109.content: Part of Architecture, for contributors and the curious. Nothing here is needed to use FLARE. A schedule answers one question: what should a light look like right now? It’s a Python object (ScheduleCoordinator), the entities that hold its settings, and the entities that publish its answer.

110.title: Where a schedule’s numbers live
110.content: A schedule has no stored configuration of its own. Its settings are 21 entities, each restoring its own value across a restart: . | five time entities, the boundaries: morning_time, day_time, evening_earliest_time, evening_latest_time, night_time | sixteen number entities: each phase’s brightness and Kelvin, and how many minutes before the next phase each starts easing towards it | . They live in entity state rather than subentry.data because changing subentry data reloads the whole entry. That also makes them ordinary HA entities: an automation can change Evening’s colour with number.set_value, and the dashboard’s sliders are just these numbers. read_schedule() is the one place that reads them. It finds each entity by unique id (ScheduleInstance.current_id()), so a renamed entity is still read. It leaves out anything unreachable, and each caller decides what that means: the curve falls back to the default, and an export omits the value.

112.title: The curve maths (schedule/curve.py)
112.content: Pure functions, with every literal a named default (DEFAULT_CURVE_VALUES, DEFAULT_SCHEDULE_HOURS). Which phase is it? . phase_at() walks the boundaries in order: before Morning is Night, then Morning, Day, Evening, and after the Night boundary it’s Night again. A Night earlier than Morning is after midnight (_night_clock). It’s tomorrow’s boundary, and Evening runs on through midnight until it. Every timestamp is shifted onto a clock where Night comes after Evening before comparing. gantt dateFormat HH:mm axisFormat %H:%M title Night at 01:00, after midnight section Phase Evening (from yesterday) :e0, 00:00, 01:00 Night :n, 01:00, 06:00 Morning :m, 06:00, 08:00 Day :d, 08:00, 17:30 Evening :e, 17:30, 23:59 . Above, Evening runs from sunset to 01:00, and the 00:00 to 01:00 slot is still yesterday’s Evening. Without _night_clock a 01:00 Night would skip Evening altogether and start at sunset. How bright, how warm? . Each phase holds its own value, then eases linearly to the next phase’s value over its last <phase>_<brightness|kelvin>_transition minutes, so the next value arrives exactly at the boundary. The transition is clamped to the phase’s length; Day’s Kelvin default (1440 minutes) spans the whole of Day. With the default settings and a 17:30 sunset, brightness runs: . | From | To | Brightness | . | 22:00 | 05:30 | 80 (Night) | . | 05:30 | 06:00 | 80 → 255, Night’s 30-minute transition | . | 06:00 | 16:25 | 255 (Morning, then Day) | . | 16:25 | 17:30 | 255 → 180, Day’s 65-minute transition | . | 17:30 | 21:00 | 180 (Evening) | . | 21:00 | 22:00 | 180 → 80, Evening’s 60-minute transition | . day_phase is a parameter, not worked out from the time, because a manual override passes a phase the clock disagrees with. So every ramp clamps its factor and can’t extrapolate. Strictly outside its own span, an overridden phase returns its own value. RGB is Kelvin converted, through HA’s color_temperature_to_rgb with a round-half-up wrapper that matches the card’s Math.round. Kept in step with JavaScript . The dashboard’s chart and the docs playground draw the same curve in JavaScript. tests/unit/dashboard/test_js_parity.py holds phase_at, phase_marks and the Night-after-midnight rule in step across the two.

113.title: The phase override
113.content: stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Auto Auto --> Overridden: select a phase<br/>(baseline = computed_phase) Overridden --> Auto: select Auto Overridden --> Auto: computed_phase moves past the baseline<br/>(unless Sticky is on) Overridden --> Overridden: refresh, same computed_phase . The select stores the computed phase at the moment it was set (the baseline). The override clears once the clock’s phase moves on, so it lasts until the next natural boundary rather than for a fixed time. switch.<slug>_sticky_phase_override turns the clearing off. The baseline isn’t saved across a restart; a restored override takes the phase at startup as its baseline.

114.title: How a room hears about it
114.content: The blueprint reads a schedule two ways: . | the Phase event entity triggers a room on a real phase change (and once after setup, so a restart repaints every room). A trigger can’t look up a device’s entities, which is why it’s an event entity on the schedule’s device and not a template. | the schedule sensor’s attributes, read in variables: for brightness, color_temp and rgb_color. | . Between phase changes, the curve still moves within a phase, so rooms also update on their area’s tick.

115.title: Export and import
115.content: schedule/transfer.py writes a schedule as YAML keyed by phase, and reads it back. The flare.export_schedule and flare.import_schedule services use it, as do Reconfigure, the transfer card and the docs playground. | Parsed with PyYAML’s BaseLoader, so every scalar is a string. YAML 1.1 would read an unquoted 06:30 as the base-60 number 390. | Written by hand so every time is quoted. docs/assets/js/schedule-yaml.js is the playground’s copy, held to it by test_schedule_yaml_parity.py. | Import parses the whole document first, then sets each value through time.set_value / number.set_value, exactly as moving a slider does. | .

116.title: Services
116.content: FLARE’s services are Home Assistant actions that any automation or script can call, and the blueprint is built on them. Developer Tools → Actions shows the same fields as this page. | Service | Description | . | flare.apply_lighting | Sets lights to a brightness and colour, leaving alone any that someone else has changed | . | flare.turn_off | Turns lights off, recording that FLARE did it | . | flare.compute_lighting_groups | Works out what apply_lighting would send, without sending it | . | flare.compute_curve | The curve’s brightness and colour for any moment | . | flare.claims_check | Whether FLARE would leave each light alone | . | flare.claims_record | Records a change you’re about to make as FLARE’s | . | flare.claims_clear | Discards claims, so FLARE sets the lights again | . | flare.claims_override | Marks lights as changed by someone else, so FLARE leaves them alone | . | flare.compute_scene_coverage | Which of a room’s lights a scene sets | . | flare.resolve_target | The entities a target reaches | . | flare.export_schedule | A schedule’s settings as YAML | . | flare.import_schedule | Sets a schedule from YAML | . In the field tables, a schedule is passed as its device ID. In a template, device_id() of any of its entities gives you that, such as device_id('sensor.home_flare') for the Home schedule. A room is passed as room_id, usually the calling automation’s own entity ID, {{ this.entity_id }}; see rooms. 117.title: flare.apply_lighting
117.content: Use this action to set lights to a brightness and colour temperature, turning on any that are off. It skips lights that are unavailable, already close to the target, or changed by something else (see override protection). action: flare.apply_lighting data: entities: [light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2] brightness: "{{ state_attr('sensor.home_flare', 'brightness') }}" color_temp_kelvin: "{{ state_attr('sensor.home_flare', 'color_temp') }}" transition: 2 brightness_levels: { light.kitchen_2: 60 } room_id: "{{ this.entity_id }}" . This sets both kitchen lights to the Home schedule’s current colour temperature, with light.kitchen_1 at the schedule’s brightness and light.kitchen_2 at 60. Fields . | Field | Required | Description | . | brightness0–255 | unless every light has a level | The brightness for every light that isn’t in brightness_levels. 0 turns the lights off, as it does for light.turn_on. | . | brightness_levelsmap of entity ID to level | no | A brightness for individual lights, in place of brightness. See brightness levels. | . | color_temp_kelvinKelvin | yes | The colour temperature. | . | entitieslist of light entity IDs | yes | The lights to set. | . | forceboolean; default false | no | Sets every light, including ones someone else has changed. The change is still recorded as FLARE’s. | . | min_brightness_changepercent, 0–25; default from FLARE → Settings → Configure | no | A light within this percentage of the target brightness, or 2 if that’s more, isn’t sent anything, and still matches its claim. See tolerances. | . | min_color_temp_changemireds, 0–50; default from FLARE → Settings → Configure | no | A light within this many mireds of the target colour temperature isn’t sent anything, and still matches its claim. For an rgb_color target, the channels’ differences added together can be up to twice this. | . | prefer_rgb_colorboolean; default false | no | Sends rgb_color instead of color_temp_kelvin to lights that support RGB. | . | rgb_color[r, g, b] or null | no | The colour for RGB lights when prefer_rgb_color is on. The schedule sensor’s rgb_color attribute is the colour temperature converted to RGB. Ignored if prefer_rgb_color is off. | . | room_entitieslist of light entity IDs | no | The room’s lights, which FLARE releases together once none of them is on. Without it, the lights this room’s calls have set. | . | room_idtext | no | The room to record the change for, usually the calling automation: {{ this.entity_id }}. Without it, FLARE records nothing and doesn’t leave any light alone. See rooms. | . | transitionseconds, 0–300 | yes | How long the change takes. Two-step bulbs spend half of it on brightness and half on colour. | . | two_step_labellabel ID; default no_combined_transition | no | Lights or devices with this label are sent two commands. See two-step bulbs. | . Brightness levels . | Value | Effect | . | 1–255 | Sets the light to this brightness. | . | 0 | Turns the light off. | . | null or false | Leaves the light alone, whether it’s on or off. | . Response data . Optional. With response_variable, the response is what was sent, in the same shape as compute_lighting_groups returns.

118.title: flare.turn_off
118.content: Use this action to turn lights off and record that FLARE did it, so FLARE doesn’t treat them as changed by someone else. action: flare.turn_off data: entities: [light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2] transition: 15 room_id: "{{ this.entity_id }}" . Fields . | Field | Required | Description | . | entitieslist of light entity IDs | yes | The lights to turn off. | . | room_entitieslist of light entity IDs | no | The room’s lights, as for apply_lighting. | . | room_idtext | no | The room to record the turn-off for. Without it, FLARE records nothing. | . | transitionseconds, 0–300; default 0 | no | How long the change takes. | . Good to know . | It turns off every light it’s given, including lights someone else has changed. To turn off only the lights FLARE is still setting, call claims_check first. | Use it rather than light.turn_off, which records nothing, so FLARE would treat the lights as switched off by someone else. | .

119.title: flare.compute_lighting_groups
119.content: Use this action to find out what apply_lighting would send, without sending it. It takes the same fields as apply_lighting, except transition. action: flare.compute_lighting_groups data: entities: [light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2] brightness: 200 color_temp_kelvin: 3200 brightness_levels: { light.kitchen_2: 100 } response_variable: plan . Response data . groups is a list with one entry for each brightness being sent, and each entry has these fields: . | brightness: The brightness the group’s lights are sent, or 0 for lights being turned off. | needing_off: Lights that need turning off. | combined: Lights sent brightness and colour temperature in one command. | two_step: Lights sent brightness and colour temperature as two commands. | combined_rgb, two_step_rgb: The same, for lights sent rgb_color. | . Lights that are unavailable, already close to the target, or changed by someone else aren’t in any list. groups: - brightness: 200 needing_off: [] combined: [light.kitchen_1] two_step: [] combined_rgb: [] two_step_rgb: [] - brightness: 100 needing_off: [] combined: [] two_step: [light.kitchen_2] combined_rgb: [] two_step_rgb: [] .

120.title: flare.compute_curve
120.content: Use this action to work out the curve’s phase, brightness and colour at any moment, for phase start times and curve settings you give it, without needing a schedule. action: flare.compute_curve data: morning: "{{ today_at('06:00') | as_timestamp }}" day: "{{ today_at('08:00') | as_timestamp }}" evening: "{{ today_at('18:00') | as_timestamp }}" night: "{{ today_at('22:00') | as_timestamp }}" evening_brightness: 150 at: "{{ today_at('20:00') | as_timestamp }}" response_variable: curve . Fields . | Field | Required | Description | . | atUnix timestamp; default now | no | The moment to work out the values for. | . | day, evening, morning, nightUnix timestamp | yes | When each phase starts today. If night is earlier than morning, Night starts after midnight, and Evening runs until then. | . | <phase>_brightness0–255; default Morning 255, Day 255, Evening 180, Night 80 | no | The phase’s brightness. | . | <phase>_brightness_transitionminutes, 0–1440; default Morning 60, Day 65, Evening 60, Night 30 | no | How long before the phase ends its brightness starts changing to the next phase’s. | . | <phase>_kelvinKelvin, 1000–10000; default Morning 6667, Day 6667, Evening 3200, Night 2700 | no | The phase’s colour temperature. | . | <phase>_kelvin_transitionminutes, 0–1440; default Morning 60, Day 1440, Evening 60, Night 30 | no | How long before the phase ends its colour temperature starts changing to the next phase’s. | . <phase> is morning, day, evening or night, so evening_brightness is Evening’s brightness. The defaults are the values a new schedule starts with, and transitions explains how a transition shapes the curve. Response data . | phase: Morning, Day, Evening or Night. | brightness: The brightness, 0–255. | kelvin: The colour temperature, in Kelvin. | rgb_color: The colour temperature converted to RGB, as [r, g, b]. | . phase: Evening brightness: 150 kelvin: 3200 rgb_color: [255, 184, 123] .

121.title: flare.claims_check
121.content: Use this action to find out whether FLARE would leave each light alone, for lights you set yourself with override protection. It changes nothing. action: flare.claims_check data: entities: [light.kitchen_1] response_variable: check . Fields . | Field | Required | Description | . | entitieslist of light entity IDs | yes | The lights to check. | . | min_brightness_changepercent, 0–25; default from FLARE → Settings → Configure | no | A light within this percentage of a claimed brightness, or 2 if that’s more, matches it. | . | min_color_temp_changemireds, 0–50; default from FLARE → Settings → Configure | no | A light within this many mireds of a claimed colour temperature matches it. For a claimed RGB colour, the channels’ differences added together can be up to twice this. | . Response data . results is keyed by entity ID, and each entry has these fields: . | blocked: true if FLARE would leave the entity alone. | status: controlled, overridden, mismatched, untracked, off or unavailable. See inspecting tracked state. | matched_via: Which claim the entity matched, and how: latest-context, latest-value, observed-context or observed-value. null if it matched neither. | rooms: The rooms the light is one of, by the room_id each named. | . results: light.kitchen_1: blocked: false status: controlled matched_via: latest-context rooms: [automation.kitchen_lighting] .

122.title: flare.claims_record
122.content: Use this action to record a change you’re about to make, so a later claims_check treats it as FLARE’s. Call it just before you change the entities, with the values you’re about to send. action: flare.claims_record data: entities: [light.kitchen_1] room_id: "{{ this.entity_id }}" targets: light.kitchen_1: { brightness: 200, color_temp_kelvin: 3000 } . Fields . | Field | Required | Description | . | entitieslist of light entity IDs | yes | The lights you’re about to change. | . | room_entitieslist of light entity IDs | no | The room’s lights, as for apply_lighting. | . | room_idtext | yes | The room to record the claim for, usually your automation: {{ this.entity_id }}. | . | targetsmap of entity ID to values | no | What you’re about to send each entity: brightness and either color_temp_kelvin or rgb_color. | . Response data . Optional. recorded lists the entities a claim was recorded for. Good to know . | Without targets, FLARE can only match the change by its context, which Home Assistant drops after five seconds. A bulb that’s slower than that to report back is then treated as changed by someone else. | A light running an effect that keeps changing its colour won’t match its claim. Use a scene for it instead, or hand it over with a null brightness in the blueprint. | .

123.title: flare.claims_clear
123.content: Use this action to discard claims, so FLARE sets the entities again on its next update. It’s for a light that’s overridden in a room that never goes fully dark. FLARE’s Clear button does the same for every light. action: flare.claims_clear data: entities: [light.kitchen_1] . Fields . | Field | Required | Description | . | entitieslist of light entity IDs | yes | The lights to clear. | . Response data . Optional. cleared lists the entities that had a claim to discard.

124.title: flare.claims_override
124.content: Use this action to mark lights as changed by someone else, so FLARE leaves them alone. You don’t usually need it. When something other than FLARE changes a light that FLARE is driving, FLARE notices on its own and leaves the light alone. It’s for lights FLARE isn’t driving yet, such as when your automation turns lights on in a dark room and you want FLARE to leave them as they are. Without it, the room’s FLARE automation sets those lights back to the curve on its next update. It marks each entity whether it’s on or off. A light marked this way stays overridden until its room goes dark, its claims are cleared, or a forced flare.apply_lighting takes it back. Flares call it before turning a room off or setting it to a brightness or colour. action: flare.claims_override data: entities: [light.kitchen_1] room_id: "{{ this.entity_id }}" . Fields . | Field | Required | Description | . | entitieslist of light entity IDs | yes | The lights to mark. | . | room_entitieslist of light entity IDs | no | The room’s lights, as for apply_lighting. | . | room_idtext | yes | The room that releases them once it’s dark, usually the automation driving them. | . Response data . Optional. overridden lists the entities passed in.

125.title: flare.compute_scene_coverage
125.content: Use this action to find out which of a set of lights a scene sets, so you can apply the scene and set the other lights yourself. action: flare.compute_scene_coverage data: scene_entity_id: scene.kitchen_night scope_entities: [light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2, light.kitchen_strip] target_entities: [light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2] response_variable: coverage . Fields . | Field | Required | Description | . | scene_entity_idscene entity ID | yes | The scene to check. | . | scope_entitieslist of entity IDs | yes | Every entity the scene is allowed to set, usually the room’s lights and other entities on the same devices. | . | target_entitieslist of entity IDs | yes | The lights to check. | . Response data . | scene_valid: true if the scene exists and every entity it sets is in scope_entities. | scene_active: The same as scene_valid. | covered_entities: The entities the scene sets. | uncovered_entities: The entries in target_entities that the scene doesn’t set. If scene_valid is false, this is all of them. | . scene_active: true scene_valid: true covered_entities: [light.kitchen_1] uncovered_entities: [light.kitchen_2] .

126.title: flare.resolve_target
126.content: Use this action to get the list of entities that an action on a target would reach, such as the lights in an area. action: flare.resolve_target target: area_id: kitchen response_variable: kitchen . Fields . It takes a target, as an action such as light.turn_on does: any mix of entity_id, device_id, area_id, floor_id and label_id. Response data . | entities: Every entity the target reaches, of any domain, sorted. Home Assistant decides which entities those are, in the same way as when you call an action on that target: . | An entity you name directly is always included. | An entity reached through a device, area, floor or label is left out if it’s hidden. | An entity reached through a device, area or floor is also left out if it’s a configuration or diagnostic entity. If a label is on the entity itself, it’s kept. | . | . entities: [binary_sensor.kitchen_motion, light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2] .

127.title: flare.export_schedule
127.content: Use this action to get a schedule’s settings as YAML, in the format described under copying a schedule. action: flare.export_schedule data: schedule_device_id: "{{ device_id('sensor.home_flare') }}" response_variable: exported . Fields . | Field | Required | Description | . | schedule_device_idschedule device ID | yes | The schedule to export. | . Response data . | schedule: The schedule as YAML text, keyed by phase. | .

128.title: flare.import_schedule
128.content: Use this action to set a schedule from YAML, in the format described under copying a schedule. action: flare.import_schedule data: schedule_device_id: "{{ device_id('sensor.home_flare') }}" schedule: night: time: "23:00" . This moves the start of Night to 23:00 and leaves every other setting as it is. Fields . | Field | Required | Description | . | scheduleYAML text, or YAML written in the call | yes | The settings to apply, keyed by phase. Any setting it leaves out keeps its current value. | . | schedule_device_idschedule device ID | yes | The schedule to set. | . Good to know . | If any part of schedule has an error, such as an unknown setting, an invalid time or a value out of range, none of it is applied, and the error message says what’s wrong. | .

129.title: Two-step bulbs
129.content: Some bulbs can’t change brightness and colour temperature in one command: they jump to the new value, or ignore one of the two. FLARE sends these bulbs two commands, brightness first and then colour, each taking half the transition. It recognises them in two ways: . | By make and model, from the Two-step bulb models field under FLARE → Settings → Configure. It holds one pattern per line, matched case-insensitively against "<manufacturer> <model>", and * matches anything, so *TRADFRI bulb* and IKEA* both work. The field is pre-filled with FLARE’s default patterns. Your saved list replaces those defaults entirely, so you can remove a pattern as well as add one. If you save the field empty, FLARE uses the defaults again. | By label: give the light or its device a label created with the name no_combined_transition. FLARE matches the label’s ID, which comes from the name it was created with, so renaming another label to this won’t work. | . Once you’ve saved your own list, a later FLARE release that adds a pattern won’t change it, so you’ll need to add new bulbs yourself. Keep patterns specific, because a bulb that doesn’t need two commands transitions less smoothly when it gets them.

130.title: Services and grouping
130.content: Part of Architecture, for contributors and the curious. Nothing here is needed to use FLARE. Everything FLARE does is a service anyone can call. The blueprint is one caller, not the only one, so each service is written as a standalone tool. The field contracts live in services.yaml and the services reference. This page is about what happens inside them.

131.title: The twelve services
131.content: | Service | Kind | Registered by | Module | . | compute_curve | pure planner | Settings entry | services/handlers.py | . | compute_lighting_groups | pure planner | Settings entry | services/handlers.py | . | compute_scene_coverage | pure planner | Settings entry | services/handlers.py | . | apply_lighting | writes | Settings entry | services/handlers.py | . | turn_off | writes | Settings entry | services/handlers.py | . | claims_check | claims | Settings entry | services/handlers.py | . | claims_record | claims | Settings entry | services/handlers.py | . | claims_clear | claims | Settings entry | services/handlers.py | . | claims_override | claims | Settings entry | services/handlers.py | . | resolve_target | lookup | async_setup (always) | services/targets.py | . | export_schedule | schedules | async_setup (always) | services/schedules.py | . | import_schedule | schedules | async_setup (always) | services/schedules.py | . The handlers are thin adapters. They read HA state into the pure planners (grouping.py, scenes.py, curve.py, override_protection.py) and send the result. The last three need nothing of an entry, so they exist as soon as the integration loads.

132.title: apply_lighting, from call to bulb
132.content: sequenceDiagram autonumber participant C as Caller (room automation) participant H as apply_lighting participant G as build_groups (pure) participant L as EntityLookup participant R as ClaimRegistry participant B as light.turn_on / turn_off C->>H: entities, brightness, kelvin,<br/>levels, transition, room_id H->>H: without_flares(entities) H->>G: plan(call) G->>L: reachable? overridden? already set?<br/>two-step model or label? L->>R: record(entity) (only with a room_id) G-->>H: groups H->>H: one send per non-empty list:<br/>off, combined, combined RGB,<br/>two-step, two-step RGB H->>R: async_record(written lights, context, targets) H->>R: adopt(already_set lights) H->>B: asyncio.gather(all sends) H-->>C: groups (optional response) . Steps 3 to 9 contain no await. The registry’s writers are callbacks, so the plan and the claims are one atomic step: no state change can arrive between deciding to write a light and recording that FLARE did.

133.title: build_groups: lights to service calls
133.content: The goal is the fewest calls that move every light that needs it, and nothing that doesn’t. flowchart TB E["entities"] --> BK["bucket by the brightness each is sent:<br/>its level, else brightness;<br/>0 is off, null/false is hands-off (dropped)"] BK --> OFFQ{"bucket brightness 0?"} OFFQ -->|"yes"| OFF["needing_off:<br/>reachable, not already off,<br/>not overridden"] OFFQ -->|"no"| RGBQ{"prefer RGB and<br/>bulb supports it?"} RGBQ -->|"yes"| RGB["target_rgb:<br/>{brightness, rgb_color}"] RGBQ -->|"no"| CT["target:<br/>{brightness, color_temp_kelvin}"] RGB --> ROUTE CT --> ROUTE ROUTE["route(lights, target)"] --> W["writable:<br/>reachable and not overridden"] W --> AS{"on and already<br/>close enough?"} AS -->|"yes"| ALR["already_set<br/>(adopted, not sent)"] AS -->|"no"| TSQ{"two-step model<br/>or label?"} TSQ -->|"yes"| TS["two_step / two_step_rgb"] TSQ -->|"no"| CB["combined / combined_rgb"] . One closeness, for both questions: is this still what FLARE set? and should FLARE bother sending? The tolerances are 5 % of the target brightness and 5 mireds by default, from the Settings entry’s options; a call may pass its own. An RGB target’s channel differences are summed and allowed twice the colour tolerance. Device rounding has fixed floors: 2 brightness points for dim targets, Kelvins that floor to the same mired, and 4 summed for RGB. 5 % and 5 mireds are about one just-noticeable difference, so a light too close to be worth a write is never someone else’s change either. Both go through tracking/matching.shows(), the one place a light’s reported values are compared with a target (see Claims and override protection). Brightness is clamped to 255 (MAX_BRIGHTNESS) before it’s compared. light.turn_on silently clamps, so an unclamped target would never read as reached, and FLARE would resend it every tick. Two-step bulbs . Some bulbs (IKEA TRADFRI) drop the colour if brightness and colour change in one transition. A light goes two-step if its device’s "<manufacturer> <model>" matches a glob in the Settings entry’s Two-step bulb models, or it carries the no_combined_transition label. sequenceDiagram participant H as apply_lighting participant B as Bulb Note over H: contexts made up front:<br/>brightness ctx (secondary),<br/>colour ctx (primary) H->>B: turn_on(brightness, transition: T/2)<br/>context: brightness ctx Note over H: asyncio.sleep(T/2) H->>B: turn_on(brightness + colour, transition: T/2)<br/>context: colour ctx . Both context ids go into the claim, and a report under either counts as FLARE’s. The sleep is why claims are recorded first: a mode: restart can cancel the run mid-sleep.

134.title: turn_off
134.content: flare.turn_off records {"state": "off"} as each light’s target, then calls light.turn_off, as one operation and with no override protection: a room emptying takes hand-set lights too. The off target is what tells FLARE’s off from anyone else’s once the context has expired. Callers mustn’t split it back into a claim and a bare light.turn_off.

135.title: Adoption
135.content: A light that’s already on and showing what apply_lighting would send gets no write. If it’s unclaimed, ClaimRegistry.adopt() claims it as it is, with its current context and values, and adds it to the room. Otherwise, a Clear in a lit room would leave most lights unclaimed, and a hand change to one would go unnoticed.

136.title: resolve_target
136.content: flare.resolve_target returns the entities a target reaches by HA’s own rule (helpers/target.py, async_extract_referenced_entity_ids, with expand_group=False). It’s the same rule light.turn_on area_id: uses and a flare’s membership uses. Templates can’t apply it: they can see is_hidden_entity, but not entity_category, and device_entities() misses child devices. target_entities() in the same module is what area setup calls to decide which areas have lights.

137.title: Scene coverage
137.content: compute_scene_coverage works out which of the room’s lights a scene covers (scenes.py, generic, nothing lighting-specific). A scene counts as active only if it exists and everything it covers is within scope (the room’s entities plus every entity on each light’s device). The blueprint then sends the curve to the lights the scene doesn’t cover, and releases the claims on the ones it does.

138.title: Setup and upgrades
138.content: Part of Architecture, for contributors and the curious. Nothing here is needed to use FLARE. How FLARE gets from “Add Integration” to rooms that light themselves, and how it keeps an installed blueprint current.

139.title: The main flow
139.content: FlareConfigFlow (config_flow.py) is the integration page’s main button. The first time it sets everything up. After that, it’s Set up area. flowchart TB U(["Add Integration / Set up area"]) --> Q{"Schedules entry exists?"} Q -->|"no: first setup"| S["schedules:<br/>Home, one per floor, or Custom"] S -->|"Custom, or floor names<br/>that fail the checks"| SN["schedule_names"] S --> CE SN --> CE["_create_entries():<br/>Schedules, Settings, Flares<br/>via SOURCE_IMPORT"] CE --> AU{"automations menu<br/>(skipped with no lit areas)"} AU -->|"Skip for now"| SUM AU -->|"set up areas"| AR Q -->|"yes"| AR["areas:<br/>a schedule dropdown per area,<br/>grouped by floor"] AR --> AS["area_setup.async_set_up_areas():<br/>an automation per area"] AS --> FM{"flares menu"} FM -->|"Skip"| SUM FM -->|"pick rooms"| FR["flare_rooms:<br/>room flares, all ticked"] FR --> SUM(["abort: setup_complete / areas_set_up,<br/>with a summary"]) . | The entries are created through SOURCE_IMPORT: the flow starts a hidden import flow for each missing one. Each entry type has a fixed unique id (flare_schedules, flare_tracking, flare_flares), so there’s only ever one of each, and deleting one and adding it back works. | The flow ends on an abort carrying a summary, never on an entry. HA’s “integration added” dialog would put every device of the entry the flow completes on through a rename-and-place form, with no way to suppress it. | First setup raises a repair linking to a page reload, since a page open during setup never loads the dashboard’s JavaScript (see Dashboard internals). | .

140.title: Subentry and options flows
140.content: | Flow | Where | Does | . | SensorSubentryFlow | Schedules entry, Add schedule | a new schedule; Reconfigure shows it as YAML to copy out or replace, and applying sets the entities, leaving the subentry untouched | . | FlareSubentryFlow | Flares entry, Add flare | a flare over a FLARE-blueprint automation, or a custom one by input | . | FlareOptionsFlow | Settings entry, Configure | tick interval and gap, minimum change, two-step models | . Reconfiguring a subentry ends with async_update_and_abort. Subentry changes don’t reload an entry by themselves, so each entry has an update listener (_async_reload_entry) that does. It yields once (asyncio.sleep(0)), so several subentries added in one go, as area setup does, reload the entry once.

141.title: Area setup (area_setup.py)
141.content: sequenceDiagram participant F as config flow participant A as area_setup participant Y as automations.yaml participant HA as automation integration F->>A: async_set_up_areas({area: schedule}) A->>A: one config per area:<br/>use_blueprint flare/flare.yaml,<br/>schedule device, room_target {area_id} A->>HA: async_validate_config_item (each) A->>Y: read, append, write_utf8_file_atomic A->>HA: automation.reload alt the entities appear A->>A: put each automation in its area,<br/>label it FLARE else they don't (configuration.yaml<br/>doesn't include the file) A->>Y: restore the original text, byte for byte end . It writes automations.yaml the way HA’s own automation editor does (components/config/automation.py), because there’s no public API for it. A lock in hass.data keeps two setups from interleaving. | Which areas are offered: every area holding a light by HA’s own rule (target_entities({"area_id": ...})), so an area with only hidden or categorised lights isn’t offered. | “Already set up” means an automation labelled FLARE sits in the area. That only unticks the area: running Set up area again adds another automation. | Not handled yet: a failure part-way leaves what was already created. | .

142.title: Keeping the blueprint current
142.content: HA never installs a custom integration’s blueprints, so FLARE checks for its own once HA has started (async_at_started), from the Settings entry. flowchart TB start(["HA started"]) --> ours{"any blueprint<br/>named FLARE?"} ours -->|"no"| miss["repair: blueprint_not_installed<br/>Fix installs flare/flare.yaml"] ours -->|"yes"| used{"used by an automation,<br/>and stamped older than<br/>this release, or in<br/>another language?"} used -->|"yes"| old["repair: outdated_blueprint<br/>Fix writes the shipped file<br/>over each stale copy"] used -->|"no"| ok(["clear both repairs"]) . | Ours is recognised by name, “FLARE”. Only copies an automation uses count as outdated: HA never removes an unused copy, and a repair about one nobody reads couldn’t be silenced. | The version stamp is in the blueprint’s description, since the blueprint: block is a closed schema and the description survives every import route. It’s 0.0.0-dev in source. scripts/release.py writes the real version into each release’s zip, along with the manifest and BLUEPRINT_VERSION. | The blueprint is written in HA’s language (blueprint_translation.py). HA has no translations for a blueprint, so _shipped() swaps in each input’s text from blueprints/translations/<language>.yaml before saving it; keys, defaults and selectors stay, and select options keep their English values under a translated label. The stamp names the language (Blueprint version 2.0.0 (de)), so a copy in another language than HA’s counts as outdated and Fix rewrites it. A copy stamped without one reads as English. | A blueprint that fails to load comes back from async_get_blueprints() as the exception itself, hence isinstance rather than a None check. | .

143.title: Migrations
143.content: async_migrate_entry handles version 3. Minor version 1 to 2 is FLARE 2.0: it removes the old zone subentries (taking their devices, entities and claims with them) and retitles a “Zones” entry “Settings”. Dropping the claims fails open, since FLARE takes every room back on its next update.

144.title: Getting a build onto a real house
144.content: HACS installs only released zips, so a development build is written over an installed release file by file. The steps are in CLAUDE.md (“Getting a build onto the live instance”). Try it in the sandbox first.

145.title: Templates
145.content: The blueprint’s three template inputs cover what its other settings can’t: a light that depends on something other than the phase, or a single light treated differently from the rest of the room. This page covers how each one works, with examples. The Blueprint page lists what each one accepts. On this page . | Brightness Template . | Dimming a light while the TV is on | Dimming some lights in the evening | Leaving a light to another automation | One level for the whole room | A level that follows the curve | 0 or null? | . | Idle Brightness Template . | One lamp as the nightlight | A whole-room nightlight | A nightlight that follows the sun | . | Scene Template | .

146.title: Brightness Template
146.content: Returns the brightness each light should sit at, as a mapping from entity ID to a level: . | Value | Effect | . | 1–255 | The light sits at this brightness, on the same scale as the phase brightnesses | . | 0 | The light is turned off | . | null or false | FLARE leaves the light alone entirely, on or off | . A light the template doesn’t mention follows the curve as usual, so return {} when the template has nothing to change. Dimming a light while the TV is on . {{ {'light.lounge_ceiling': 40} if is_state('media_player.tv', 'playing') else {} }} . While the TV plays, the ceiling light sits at 40 and the rest of the room follows the curve. Add media_player.tv to Additional Triggers so the room changes as soon as the TV starts or stops, rather than at the next update. Dimming some lights in the evening . {% set phase = states('sensor.home_flare') %} {% if phase == 'Evening' %} {{ {'light.kitchen_1': 20, 'light.kitchen_2': 20} }} {% elif phase == 'Night' %} {{ {'light.kitchen_1': 5, 'light.kitchen_2': 5} }} {% else %} {{ {} }} {% endif %} . The rest of the kitchen follows the curve; these two sit lower once Evening starts. Leaving a light to another automation . {{ {'light.kitchen_strip': none} if states('sensor.home_flare') in ['Evening', 'Night'] else {} }} . In the evening another automation runs a gradient on the kitchen strip, so this hands the strip over during Evening and Night and FLARE leaves it alone. FLARE won’t turn it off when the room empties either; the other automation needs to do that. One level for the whole room . A single number applies to every light in the room: . {{ 40 if is_state('media_player.tv', 'playing') else none }} . none here means “no opinion”, so the room follows the curve when the TV is off. A level that follows the curve . A level is fixed: the light stays at it for as long as the template returns it, whatever the time of day. To keep a light at, say, half the room’s brightness, read the curve and scale it: . {{ {'light.lounge_ceiling': state_attr('sensor.home_flare', 'brightness') | int * 0.5} }} . 0 or null? . 0 turns the light off but keeps it FLARE’s, so it comes back on with the rest of the room. null hands the light over completely: FLARE doesn’t touch it at all, so it isn’t turned off when the room empties either, and whatever controls it has to do that instead. The template wins over the Lights Off During lists for any light it names.

147.title: Idle Brightness Template
147.content: Returns what each light dims to when the room is empty, instead of going dark. It takes the same values as Brightness Template, and wins over the per-phase Idle Brightness settings for any light it names. One lamp as the nightlight . {{ {'light.landing_lamp': 20} }} . With the phase settings at 0, this lamp stays at 20 when the landing empties and every other light goes out. When a phase’s setting is 0, only the lights the template names have an idle brightness in that phase. So a template naming one lamp makes that lamp the room’s only nightlight, even if you only meant to give it a different level from the rest. To keep the rest dim too, set the phase’s Idle Brightness as well, and use the template for the one light. A whole-room nightlight . A single number applies to every light in the room: . {{ 20 }} . A nightlight that follows the sun . The Night phase starts at a fixed time, not at dark. For a hall that stays dimly lit whenever it’s dark outside, leave the four phase settings at 0 and use the sun: . {{ 10 if is_state('sun.sun', 'below_horizon') else {} }} . {} means “no opinion”, so the hall goes fully dark while the sun is up. The hall picks up the change at the next update after sunset, which can be up to a minute later. Don’t add sun.sun to Additional Triggers to make it immediate: at sunrise that would bring the lights up to the curve instead of turning them off.

148.title: Scene Template
148.content: Returns a scene’s entity ID, to hand the room to that scene instead of the curve. It wins over the per-phase scene pickers whenever it returns a scene that exists. {{ 'scene.lounge_movie' if is_state('media_player.tv', 'playing') else '' }} . Return '' for no scene. See Scenes for how a room shares itself with a scene.
